name: EPA
title: The Specter of 'Forever Chemicals' Looms Over Pennsylvania's Rural Communities
authors: Derek Harrison, Ben Seal, Amy Green
description:
The chemicals in Williams’ well are among a class of thousands known collectively as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, colloquially called “forever chemicals” because they don’t break down naturally.
In 2024, the agency established drinking water standards for six PFAS chemicals, including limits of 4 parts per trillion (ppt) for PFOA and PFOS, two of the most prominent.
That fall, the Williams’ water tested at 182.4 total ppt.
Among 80 residential wells tested by state environmental regulators during their investigation, 23 had rates above the Williams’, reaching as high as 3,612 total ppt.
Over the years, forever chemicals had been migrating from these soils into the groundwater that feeds residents’ wells and neighboring waterways.
text:
When Nicole Williams moved into her house in Pennsylvania’s North Centre Township in 2011, it was a homecoming. She’d spent the first few years of her life a half-mile down the road in Brookside Village, a tidy community of 170 mobile homes nestled between the west branch of Briar Creek and a farm that grew sweet corn and pumpkins just up the hill. Her new colonial revival with expansive views of the Susquehanna Valley’s rolling landscape was one of several houses built on land that once belonged to that farm.

Fifteen years later, Williams has three kids between 11 and 16, two English bulldogs and an in-line water filtration system in her basement whose two sturdy tanks remove the toxic chemicals leaching from the neighboring farm into her well.

The chemicals in Williams’ well are among a class of thousands known collectively as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, colloquially called “forever chemicals” because they don’t break down naturally. They were present in the sewage sludge the nearby farm received from the local water treatment plant and spread on its fields as fertilizer beginning sometime in the 1980s. For two years, the state Department of Environmental Protection has been investigating the groundwater plume emanating from the farm and around a dozen other sites in Columbia County that also utilized the sludge.

The investigation is the state’s first in the region, but the crisis in North Centre “is the tip of the iceberg,” said Lane Whigham, director of the Alliance for Aquatic Resource Monitoring—which goes by ALLARM—at Dickinson College in Carlisle. His group’s volunteers test water quality throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed, including Columbia County. The Department of Environmental Protection found elevated levels of PFAS in Briar Creek and has cautioned residents not to eat fish caught there. That warning is likely just the beginning of what’s needed, according to Whigham.

A 2023 study led by the U.S. Geological Survey found that 76 percent of Pennsylvania streams contained at least one PFAS. In 2025, the Three Rivers Waterkeeper tested 39 sites in Western Pennsylvania and found PFAS in 74 percent. When it comes to these chemicals in the state’s waterways, “it’s not a matter of ‘if’ anymore, it’s ‘how much,’” Whigham said.

Consuming high levels of PFAS—used in a wide range of industrial processes and consumer products—can pose a risk to reproductive and developmental health, hinder the body’s immune system and hormones and contribute to a variety of cancers, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

In 2024, the agency established drinking water standards for six PFAS chemicals, including limits of 4 parts per trillion (ppt) for PFOA and PFOS, two of the most prominent. That fall, the Williams’ water tested at 182.4 total ppt. PFOA in their water was eight times the EPA limit; PFOS was 32 times the limit.

Among 80 residential wells tested by state environmental regulators during their investigation, 23 had rates above the Williams’, reaching as high as 3,612 total ppt.

The worrying presence of PFAS in sewage sludge—the semi-solid, nutrient-rich material left after wastewater treatment, referred to by the waste industry as biosolids—was first identified in Maine in 2016. Well testing revealed elevated levels on a dairy farm there. The farm’s milk was also contaminated, and further testing has identified tainted water on more than 100 farms and 500 residential properties in the state.

Maine became the first state to ban the use of sludge on farmland in 2022. Pennsylvania, like nearly every other state, still allows the practice. Its use as fertilizer has long been encouraged by both federal and state agencies.

The Department of Environmental Protection estimates that 400,000 tons of sludge are applied to land in Pennsylvania annually. More than 40 percent of that total ends up on farmland, according to the National Biosolids Data Project, a group whose partners include industry members and municipal entities. Since 1997, more than 1,100 Pennsylvania farms have been permitted to apply sludge, and 740 of those permits are still active.

“If your boat is filling up with water, you need to plug the hole first,” said Stephanie Wein, a water and conservation advocate at the nonprofit PennEnvironment. “They’re just letting this stuff continue to be applied.”

The investigation in North Centre has alerted residents to the hazards in their community and stopped the consumption of tainted water. Across Pennsylvania, though, the extent of the risk posed by PFAS-contaminated sludge is unknown. A full accounting would require a testing program that could tally the toll of decades of sludge application on rural communities reliant on private wells. More than a quarter of Pennsylvania residents get their water from a private well.

An adequate response is complicated by the fact that forever chemicals are colorless, odorless and tasteless—not to mention highly persistent—and therefore undetectable without the right test.

Williams, a pediatric registered nurse, had her well water tested when she moved in, but PFAS isn’t among the pollutants typically tested, so it wasn’t caught. Now, she’s left to wonder how her children’s health might be affected by a childhood spent drinking polluted water. And she can’t help but question what’s lurking in the groundwater in rural communities across the state.

“You drive through the countryside and you no longer see these beautiful fields,” Williams said. “You look at fields and you’re like, ‘I wonder if these fields are contaminated or if these houses are OK.’”

Discovering a PFAS Crisis

The first indication that something was wrong in Columbia County came from Brookside Village, Williams’ first home.

In 2023, Pennsylvania established drinking water limits for PFOA and PFOS in public and community water systems, set at 14 and 18 ppt, respectively—both well above the federal standards announced the following year. (A statewide sampling of more than 400 public supply wells that preceded the state’s new limits found that among those where forever chemicals were detected, PFOA averaged 7.5 ppt and PFOS averaged 9.9 ppt.) Following the new regulation, water quality monitoring at Brookside in spring 2024 showed concentrations as high as 2,100 ppt.

That summer, the Department of Environmental Protection began testing private wells in the area and delivering bottled water to residents with elevated PFAS levels. The agency also identified sludge applied to the farm directly across from Brookside Village as a likely source of contamination and began sampling it and other farmland that had received sludge through the decades. Its soil contained as much as 79 ppt of PFOS. At another farm along State Route 93 a few miles north, samples reached 186 ppt.

Over the years, forever chemicals had been migrating from these soils into the groundwater that feeds residents’ wells and neighboring waterways. In all, 115 of the 285 wells sampled by the state as of May contained PFAS levels that exceeded federal limits.

To date, the department has installed point-of-entry filtration systems in 38 homes and the process is ongoing. Once the investigation is completed, residents will be on the hook for the cost of regular maintenance. At Brookside, meanwhile, management company UMH Properties has installed kitchen faucet filters to remove PFAS at the tap, but other sources within homes remain unfiltered. The company plans to install a permanent, communitywide filtration system once it is approved by the Department of Environmental Protection, according to spokesperson Ken Frydman.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Unfortunately for residents, filters and bottled water can’t reverse the potential harms of years spent drinking contaminated water. Timothy Jasinski grew up on a farm next to the tainted agricultural fields on Route 93. He recalls seeing sludge piled under plastic tarps on his neighbor’s land, waiting to be spread. On his neighbor’s side of the hedgerow, corn and soy outgrew anything his family could produce.

But he wonders now whether the sludge’s contributions to soil fertility came at an untold cost. Jasinski said some of his family members suffered from rashes that quickly cleared up after they moved away, and he’s been shocked by the number of neighbors along Route 93 who have developed cancers in recent years.

Kaylin Bower, who lives across the street from Williams, said the discovery of PFAS in the community’s groundwater has compelled residents with reproductive issues, neurological conditions and various forms of cancer to question whether it’s the source of their troubles. Her water tested at 230 total ppt, including PFOS levels nearly 40 times the federal limit.

Like other community members, Bower is still in the dark about the level of forever chemicals in her body, but she’s expecting answers soon. Geisinger, a regional health system serving Central and Northeastern Pennsylvania, is in the beginning stages of a study of those who live near one of the identified sources of pollution. The study aims to understand the link between long-term health outcomes and the levels of PFAS in individuals’ blood. Bower and Williams, who works for Geisinger, are both members of a three-person community board advising the study.

When Bower and her husband moved into their home in 2014, they were drawn by the promise of a rural lifestyle in a relatively undeveloped agricultural community. The discovery of PFAS in her water has upended her peaceful existence.

She worries about her 11-year-old son, who’s likely been consuming the chemicals since he was in the womb. And if she were to move, she suspects her property value would be limited by a stipulation on her deed, required by the state, that acknowledges her well is contaminated.

“For so many of us,” Bower said, “this was the death of a dream.”

An “Enormous” Issue for Pennsylvania

Tracy Carluccio fears it’s only a matter of time before other communities must confront the costs of Pennsylvania’s longstanding use of sewage sludge. Carluccio is deputy director of the Delaware Riverkeeper Network, which has spent years pushing the state to adopt strict limits on forever chemicals, including filing a lawsuit over the lack of action in 2019.

Given the widespread use of sludge on agricultural fields, “this is an enormous statewide issue,” she said.

In July, the Department of Environmental Protection proposed a tiered system for sludge application permits, which would create PFAS monitoring requirements for sewage treatment plants and require remediation at certain levels. Under the proposal, sludge containing less than 20 parts per billion of each PFOS and PFOA could be applied without restriction. Sludge between 20 ppb and 100 ppb could be applied at a reduced rate, and application of sludge above 100 ppb would be prohibited.

In a January 2025 draft risk assessment, the Biden-era EPA said that using sludge with as little as 1 ppb of one of the chemicals “could result in human health risks exceeding the agency’s acceptable thresholds.” The Trump administration has since criticized and backed away from those findings.

The Department of Environmental Protection’s proposed solution is “totally inadequate,” Carluccio said. Instead, she argues, the state should bring an end to sludge application, just as Maine has done. The agency declined to comment on criticism of its plan.

Until sludge application stops, the material will remain an “uncontrolled pathway” for PFAS pollution in agricultural communities, she said. “The only reason we don’t know more about it is because there hasn’t been more testing” near farms with sludge permits, she said.

In addition to a “full stop” on using sludge on farmland, Carluccio would like to see the state establish surface water standards for PFAS to protect waterways like Briar Creek and the fish that live in them—as well as those who fish those streams.

For Whigham, at ALLARM, the investigation in Columbia County raises questions about the continued manufacturing of forever chemicals that cycle through waterways and into sludge and back again.

“Are these things more important to us than clean water and clean soil and healthy food?” he said.

Facing the Consequences

Nicole Williams is still waiting to learn how much PFAS is in her bloodstream after years drinking tainted water, but she’s already pushing for answers for her community.

Seeking advice, she turned to a pair of family doctors in Maine who have treated those affected by that state’s sludge crisis. They’re exploring the potential for the cholesterol drug cholestyramine to help remove PFAS from the body. Williams’ husband is now taking the medicine in hopes it will eliminate any PFAS he’s absorbed since moving into their home.

Coupled with the study she’s advising on at the local health system, she believes it could offer her neighbors a way to respond to what they’re facing—even if it can’t undo any health impact they’ve already suffered.

Becky Garrison and her husband, Bill, have lived across from the contaminated hilltop farm since 1985. Becky Garrison grew up on a farm where spreading manure was a regular practice, so when she saw sludge piled up on the neighboring farm back in the day she didn’t think much of it. Until recently, that is.

Once they learned of the investigation, the Garrisons installed a filtration system as soon as they could, even before the state came around offering to help. Their well tested at 874 total ppt; the presence of PFOS was 125 times the federal limit.

“Who would have ever thought?” she said.

Both she and Bill have had cancer—myeloma and colon, respectively—and although she can’t know whether the PFAS in their well played a part, she also can’t help but wonder.

“After 40 years,” she said, “there’s nothing we can do.”

text:
The recently refurbished Unit 1 reactor at Ontario Power Generation’s (OPG) Darlington Nuclear is now producing critical life-saving Cobalt-60 isotopes for the world. This medical isotope is used to sterilize 40% of the world’s single-use medical devices, as well as certain food products.

OPG plans to modify Darlington’s three other units to produce these isotopes as well, helping secure a stable, reliable global supply. Additional key isotopes include Molybdenum-99, a much-needed medical isotope used in over 30 million procedures a year to detect illnesses like cancer and heart disease; Helium-3, a rare isotope used in quantum computing, neutron research, border security and medical imaging; and Tritium, used in the production of self-powered lights and medical research.

As part of the Central and Eastern Ontario Isotope Alliance, Clarington aims to unite Ontario’s isotope community and foster future opportunities to leverage the region’s strengths and assets.

In 2023, the Ontario government announced its collaboration with Ontario Power Generation to begin planning and licensing four small modular reactors (SMRs) at the Darlington Nuclear site. The construction and operation of these four 300 MW SMRs in Clarington will create and sustain 2,600 jobs, add $13.7 billion to Ontario’s GDP, and produce reliable power for 1.2 million people.

Learn more about this transformative project, the first of its kind in North America, which is paving the way for a sustainable future in Clarington.

title: Inside a Texas family's fight to stop a data center from being built on promised park land
description:
She didn’t even know what a data center was, she said.
The flyer helped her learn that plans for a data center spanning 135,000 square feet by Blueprint Data Centers – less than half a mile away from her home – had been approved.
It is now one of more than 2,000 data centers in planning stages across the United States, according to the tracking firm Cleanview.
The data center would further thrust Taylor into the massive tech and infrastructure boom in Central Texas.
Griffin’s sister is now refusing to build a home on the family lot that remains vacant, given its backyard would literally be a hop, skip and jump from the data center, Griffin said.
text:
For years, Pamela Griffin cherished a promise from a stranger that the expansive plot of land just steps from her home in Taylor, Texas, would one day become the park she and other kids in her neighborhood always wanted.

But as the land changed hands, a 14-word sentence in a 1999 deed was not carried forward, putting the property about 25 miles outside of Austin on track to become something much different: a data center.

Like other communities confronting the prospect of a data center for the first time, many residents in this town of roughly 18,000 people are concerned about noise, water use, and power shortages.

In the months since Griffin learned about the data center plans, what was supposed to be a season of slowing down in retirement has become one of organizing, attending community meetings, and speaking at public events as she wages a legal battle to protect her neighborhood, particularly the fruits of her family’s labor.

The dispute, the 58-year-old retired learning center director says, is rooted in competing interpretations of a sentence in a deed intended to ensure the land’s future as a park and in the history of who has, and has not, benefited from land ownership in the Lone Star State.

“My daddy passed this land down to us and he told us to guard this land,” she said. “He said this will always be a homestead.”

Now, a Texas appeals court is considering Griffin’s complaint, which is attempting to stop the data center project from moving forward, all while Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has launched an investigation into whether the original language on the property’s use was legally changed or removed and if it still carries legal weight today.

A community built over generations

During the 1950s and early 1960s, Griffin’s grandmother juggled working as a maid with chopping and picking cotton in Taylor, which was once known as a hub for cotton farming and for its cattle ranches.

As a Black mother, she seized an opportunity to buy real estate on the south side of Taylor after the passing of the Fair Housing Act, which made it illegal to discriminate during the sale, rental or financing of housing based on race, skin color, religion or nationality, and bought parcels for her eight children, hoping they would have a home for generations to come.

And they have.

Griffin, who had moved away after graduating high school, lives in the home her father built, where he raised six children – and where every corner seems occupied by something meaningful, all tucked away in its own space: framed photos, trinkets, and mementos.

As a girl growing up in the 1970s, Griffin recalls how her parents and other neighbors in the two-street patch of homes did not let their children play at the nearby Fannie Robinson Park after some of them started developing rashes or getting sick.

The park, which was once a city dump, became the town’s first park serving Black residents in 1955 after a Black physician negotiated with city and school officials to dedicate recreational space for children of color.

With limited places to play, an empty lot behind Griffin’s home bought by her father became an informal playground for her and other neighbors to enjoy.

It’s where they would chase baseballs or camp using cardboard boxes and bed sheets to stargaze under the deep, bright Texas stars, turning a mundane day into one filled with adventure and curiosity.

The lot bordered 87 acres owned by the descendants of Howard Bland, Sr., a prominent Taylor community leader, businessman and state lawmaker in the late 19th century. Because the children often walked into the land to retrieve stray baseballs, Griffin said, the Bland family recognized the need for a public park, telling her dad about their desire someday to turn the property into just that.

“The Blands understood the community in a way others did not and “was willing to help when nobody else was not,” Griffin said.

After both her parents passed away, Griffin returned to Taylor in 2019 feeling an innate responsibility to preserve her family’s legacy and the neighborhood that truly felt like home. Unbeknownst to Griffin, she would have to unravel what happened to the promise she had heard about for years and dedicate her retirement to fight for the future of the neighborhood.

A family’s wish was left out

When Griffin found a flyer on her front door last year, she wasn’t sure what to make of it.

“Three 45,000 SF data centers coming to your backyard,” the flyer read, along with a map and details about public hearings for Taylor residents.

She didn’t even know what a data center was, she said. Today, it’s practically all she can think about and sees as she drives around town, spotting yard signs outside homes and posters in storefront windows.

The flyer helped her learn that plans for a data center spanning 135,000 square feet by Blueprint Data Centers – less than half a mile away from her home – had been approved. It is now one of more than 2,000 data centers in planning stages across the United States, according to the tracking firm Cleanview.

The data center would further thrust Taylor into the massive tech and infrastructure boom in Central Texas. With its addition on the city’s south side, Taylor would be sandwiched between two developments powering major components of AI: chip making and data centers. On the city’s north side, there’s already a Samsung semiconductor fabrication plant, where computer chips are manufactured.

And plans for a third facility, a separate 665-acre data center called “Project Mustang,” is sparking more concerns about growth and development, particularly as it will sit outside city limits where Taylor officials don’t have the authority to stop or regulate it. The project developer had sought to annex the property to the city but withdrew its application earlier this month.

So how did the vast, serene plot of land near Griffin’s home that was promised to be a future park land suddenly become the future site of a hub for cloud collection and artificial intelligence?

In 1999, the Bland family sold the 87 acres next to Griffin’s neighborhood to the Texas Parks and Recreation Foundation for $10. The deed had a line in the grantee’s section saying the land was “to be held in trust for future use as a parkland by Williamson County.”

By 2003, the acreage was sold to a Williamson County-based parks nonprofit for $10, and sold for another $10 to the City of Taylor about seven weeks later.

After being under city ownership for a few years, the property was sold in 2009 to the city’s economic development arm, the Taylor Economic Development Corporation, in exchange for $15,000 and 39 acres, which include the 16-acre tract meant to “act as buffer between the proposed data center and the nearest neighborhood,” according to the city.

In 2025, the remaining acreage was sold to Blueprint Data Centers’ parent company for $10 million,city officials said.

The language stating the Blands’ intended use of the property is in the 1999 deed but it’s absent from all subsequent exchanges. It’s unclear why it was not included.

The City of Taylor was “unaware” of the Blands’ wishes when it acquired the land in 2003, a city spokesperson told CNN.

The Blands intended for the property to become a park, the spokesperson said, but “no legally enforceable deed restriction was placed on the property. Because there was no deed restriction, his (land donor) wishes did not transfer with the deed.”

Blueprint Data Centers, its parent company NCP Travis BPP Project LLC, and the Texas Parks and Recreation did not respond to multiple requests for comment about the project and the sales they were part of.

CNN has attempted to reach a representative for the Williamson County parks nonprofit that sold the property to the city of Taylor, as well as the two surviving members of the Bland family listed in the 1999 deed.

Determined to challenge the data center project, Griffin started doing her own research on the land and was surprised when she learned the family’s good faith gesture wasn’t just lore, it was in writing.

She and her siblings filed a lawsuit last year against NCP Travis TPP Project, LLC to permanently stop construction of the planned data center, arguing the property should remain park land under the original deed, the suit says. For them, it wasn’t about money, she said, their legal fight is about having the ability to live and thrive within the community they helped build.

“My family was willing to stand up for this community and help this community because that’s what we’re supposed to do as neighbors,” Griffin said. “We all neighbors. We supposed to take care of each other.”

A Williamson County judge dismissed their case in October 2025, saying the siblings don’t have the legal right to bring a lawsuit because they don’t own the land and have no direct financial stake in it.

Attorney Chris Osborn, who is representing the siblings, said the case was dismissed before it ever answered the bigger question of what the land was supposed to become. He said if the appeal is denied, the Bland family could potentially bring their own challenge because of their direct tie to the land.

Paxton, the state’s attorney general, announced last week his office was launching an investigation into whether the 1999 deed was lawfully modified.

“I will not allow any person or entity to disregard the rule of law or obligations owed to the public,” Paxton said in a statement. “If the Taylor data center development is unlawful, I will do everything in my power to stop it and hold those who have violated the law accountable.”

In a statement to CNN, the City of Taylor acknowledged Paxton’s investigation and said it will cooperate with the investigation but declined to comment further about the ongoing litigation.

An inheritance in question

Many Taylor residents are concerned the Blueprint Data Centers’ facility could bring a myriad of issues to the area, including light pollution, air emissions from backup generators, heavy water and electricity use, and fire risks.

In response to their concerns, city officials have said the proposed data center would use a closed-loop cooling system with minimal water demand, comply with local ordinances and include environmental and safety measures to combat some of those concerns.

Over the next 10 years, the project is estimated to generate millions of dollars in revenue, which the city says could be used to reduce property taxes, improve schools, and increase teacher salaries, among other things.

But residents like Griffin said other developments should have been prioritized, including a grocery store or a gas station, which are not easily accessible in the area.

People living near AI data centers have reported hearing a persistent humming sound coming from the building around the clock, and that’s also a major concern for Griffin. Her disabled son, who lives in nearby Round Rock, often visits to escape the bustling traffic, chain stores and rapid growth that have quickly defined many of the outskirts of Austin.

“He can walk the land … and be comfortable and it helps his disability, but once they build that thing (data center) and that noise, he can’t deal with noise,” Griffin said.

Carrie D’Anna, who also lives on the south side of Taylor and was the community member who made and delivered the flyer to Griffin’s door, said some residents have considered moving elsewhere, but not everyone has the financial means to do so. She and Griffin also doubt anyone would want to live in such proximity to a large industrial-scale development.

“Nobody has come and knocked on the door and said: ‘Hey, can we pay you to move?’ That’s not happening. Instead, we’re trapping people in poverty (against their) will,” D’Anna said.

Jerrod Kingery, a city spokesperson, said authorities are considering regulations that would restrict the construction of data centers in industrially zoned areas, require more separation between projects and establish standards in addressing water use, emissions, noise and setbacks.

For now, Griffin’s father’s dream of having more of her siblings living on the land their grandmother acquired is in jeopardy. Griffin’s sister is now refusing to build a home on the family lot that remains vacant, given its backyard would literally be a hop, skip and jump from the data center, Griffin said.

After spending their lives building a home, raising a family, acquiring land and creating wealth opportunities for their children, Griffin said her family probably never imagined future generations would have to keep fighting to protect what was left for them.

“My parents thought we was set,” Griffin said.

But Griffin says it’s all worth fighting for because some promises are meant to live beyond those who make them.

text:
Who can resist the home supply stores, nurseries, and even supermarkets all seeming to burst with eye-catching blooms, winter vegetables, shrubs for every nook and cranny, and trees? Fall is by far the best time to plant in the Valley of the Sun—the young plants have three seasons to establish before brutal heat, and you have time to assess their needs for water and shade before things get desperate (summer).

It has taken me years of trial and error, thousands of sacrificial plants, and even completing a course or two before feeling equipped to navigate the halls of temptation, and I still succumb. My gardens provide me with great joy not to mention food for my family and much needed resources for local birds and pollinators. Soon you may find yourself face to face with seemingly irresistible (and potentially expensive) choices, and it may be helpful to keep the following suggestions in mind:

Arizonans need to know their ZONE—USDA Plant Hardiness Zone, that is. Arizona is a surprisingly diverse state! Even within the Phoenix greater metro area, there are 3-4 hardiness zones meaning what will do well in north Scottsdale may be very unhappy in Buckeye. Find your planting zone here and check the plant’s tag (or Google it) before you fall in love.

Right Plant, Right Place. Prickly Pear cacti are drought tolerant, produce lovely blooms, as well as edible fruit—but you probably don’t want one right next to your pool or jungle gym. Think ahead and know how broad, tall, messy, or spiny the innocent-looking specimen will become.

Use native plants for landscaping. Once established, native plants are easy to care for and provide birds and other pollinators with resources they desperately need. Without sacrificing function or attractiveness, the below three native plants provide both practical landscaping value and ecological services.

Instead of Bougainvillea (native to South America), try Native Passion Vine (Passiflora arizonica)

Need a fast-growing vine? Trade Bougainvillea’s obnoxious thorns and worthless flowers for butterflies! A fast grower, a single Passiflora plant can spread and grow 20 by 15 feet in a year. The plant is covered with blooms from March to first freeze and produces odd-looking (edible!) fruits that ripen in summer. These strong climbers are easy to prune, and can die back to the ground in cold winters—only to resprout with vigor in early spring. The remarkable flowers bloom at night, attracting sphinx and other moths and last into the daylight hours when a colorful array of butterflies visit, most notably the Gulf Fritillary. This medium-sized orange beauty lays its tiny eggs on the foliage, and soon you’ll see caterpillars and finally more butterflies!

Instead of Hesperaloe (a native to Texas), try Chuparosa (Justicia californica)

If attracting hummingbirds is your goal, look no further! You don’t have to settle for the plant of parking lots and medians—Hesperaloe--for long-suffering hummingbird food. Chuparosa, tolerant of poor soils, sun and long hot summers, treats human observers to a feast for the eyes—and hummingbirds to a real feast! The lipstick-like blossoms bloom almost year-round and are edible—they have a delicate cucumber flavor. Seed pods look like tiny boxing gloves that will burst apart when ripe. No more need for you to clean and fill hummingbird feeders endlessly with this plant in the yard—you’ll likely see Anna’s, Black-chinned, and possibly even Costa’s come visit. Thanks to Chuparosa’s profuse blooming habitat, there is plenty for all.

Instead of Oleander, try Desert Hackberry (Celtis pallida)

Need a screen? Skip the tired old Oleander: poisonous and invasive; many older plants suffer from Oleander Leaf Scorch (OLS)—a disease common in the Phoenix valley. A great alternative is the attractive Desert Hackberry—a sturdy shrub or small tree that keeps its leaves all winter and gives you something to enjoy every season. Tiny white flowers smell delightful in spring, attracting small flower flies and other pollinators. The flowers give way to small red (edible) berries prized by birds, especially Northern Mockingbirds, House Finches, and migratory birds like White-crowned Sparrows, and Hermit Thrush. Still not convinced about the Desert Hackberry? Consider that due to the dense growth habit and thorns, this hackberry provides ideal nesting spots for our native birds—a fortress from predators. Despite all it gives, this sturdy plant requires little care, tolerates poor soil, and prefers full sun.

With all native plants, a period of patience is required—it is not recommended to expect them to thrive immediately upon installation with no action on your part. “Drought-tolerant” does not mean they are magical and can survive without water. Expect to water regularly and monitor for signs of stress. If things don’t look right, contact your local nursery sooner rather than later for advice and early intervention.

Native plants are typically harder to find than widely available non-natives, but due to increased consumer demand, they are getting easier to come by each year as is local expertise. Great resources for you include Audubon’s Native Plant Database (at which you can get a list of recommended plants based on your zip code, the Maricopa County Master Gardeners, Water Use it Wisely, and the Arizona Native Plant Society.

Now that you are armed with some suggestions and resources, you’ll likely be better able to withstand that impulse plant purchase—or at least know what you are getting into. Happy planting!

The system is designed only to put safe distance between the car and the primary power battery.

text:
Almost precisely one year ago (we’re off by just one day), Thomas reported on a novel solution for dealing with an EV battery that has caught fire: explosively yeet the thing out from under the car with sufficient force to propel it a safe distance. And what happens to anyone and anything within range of the flying, presumably on-fire battery? You can see the problem here.

So can Stellantis, and based on a new patent, the auto conglomerate has a conceptually similar but much more elegantly conceived solution to safely rid an EV or hybrid of a battery experiencing a thermal runaway or otherwise in need of quickly parting ways with the vehicle.

Instead of ejecting the battery to who knows where, Stellantis’ plan calls for dropping the battery wherever the car is stopped, and then simply driving away from it.

It’s easy to imagine how a hybrid could drive away from its street-deposited, smoking battery using its engine (provided it’s coupled to the drivetrain, and not merely powering a generator), but how would a purely electric vehicle drive away from its decoupled battery? The answer is the vehicle’s 12-volt battery.

With a typical EV running off of anywhere from 300 to 900 volts, clearly the idea is not to provide any meaningful drivability via the 12-volt battery. The system is designed only to put safe distance between the car and the primary power battery. How far? Instead of that being up to the driver, the system would “[Command] to propel the vehicle a predetermined distance away from the decoupled battery,” per the patent.

As for how the battery parts way with the vehicle, the patent describes two scenarios. Both begin with the driver activating the system via a switch, with options listed by the patent as “an electrical lever, a mechanical lever, a physical button, a touchscreen button, and a toggle switch.” Obviously, “touchscreen button” is the worst option.

Once activated, the “controller” switches the vehicle to 12-volt power and decouples the primary battery. To eject the battery from the car, two systems are proposed. The first is a “castellated frame” connection as depicted below. Sliding the frames out of registration frees the battery to drop from the vehicle.

The other, more exciting solution is to mount the battery using explosive bolts (“pyrotechnic fasteners”), which can be detonated to free the pack when things go awry (it’s not completely unheard of in cars, though this is usually used for pedestrian protection or convertible roll bar ejection). Should the system ever be green-lit for production, I wonder if both systems might be employed; the “castellated frame” as the first mechanism, with the explosive bolts as a backup in case the mechanical release fails.

It all seems perfectly reasonable and feasible, and far safer than the “fire the battery like a torpedo” concept. Only time will tell if we’ll see electric vehicles with BATTERY EJECT switches under flip-up covers, but if any automaker wants to drop the battery and drive away, they’ll need to contact Stellantis for a license first.

text:
Kenyan President William Ruto has addressed the United Nations General Assembly to demand systemic structural reform of multilateral development banks. The policy intervention targets sovereign debt sustainability frameworks and credit rating methodologies to reduce the cost of infrastructure capital across sub-Saharan clean energy projects.

At the United Nations headquarters in New York, international policy planners have received a formal framework to restructure sovereign debt distress parameters. The Kenyan executive address focused on global capital allocation rules that systematically penalise emerging infrastructure markets. For decades, high borrowing premiums and short-term amortisation schedules forced developing economies to allocate higher cash volumes to debt servicing than to domestic utility grid expansion. This fiscal drag transitions the regional climate debate from simple project generation targets to structured financial restructuring.

Sovereign debt metrics released during the summit track global public liabilities at an unprecedented $102 trillion. Ruto cited United Nations Development Programme data showing that subjective risk modelling by Western commercial rating syndicates costs African treasuries an estimated $75 billion annually in inflated interest payments. By artificially inflating the risk premium on African infrastructure assets, international capital markets effectively restrict utility-scale solar and wind developments from securing long-term, non-recourse project finance.

The financing constraints currently affect 46 developing states, where interest payments outpace total national allocations for public education and health networks. The Nairobi Declaration framework provides the underlying structural blueprint for the proposed changes, demanding independent African credit rating operations and a general capital increase for the African Development Bank. By expanding the balance sheets of regional development finance institutions, project sponsors intend to lower the volume of sovereign guarantees required to advance greenfield infrastructure portfolios.

Bilateral climate finance agreements clearing the European investment pipeline highlight a parallel international push to adjust concessional lending thresholds. Separate risk-mitigation instruments focus on establishing specialised first-loss capital pools to insulate private institutional lenders from early-stage currency convertibility hazards. By lowering the cost of hedging mechanisms, regulators aim to scale private sector debt participation across regional transmission grids.

Reforming the primary governance rules of the International Monetary Fund remains the absolute determinant of sub-Saharan infrastructure deployment velocity. The G20 independent expert panels have recommended tripling the annual lending volumes of multilateral development banks, yet executive voting quotas remain locked under post-war configurations. Ultimately, the capacity of the international coalition to implement these structural financial changes will determine whether clean energy deployment pacing matches regional industrial demand targets.

text:
Kathleen McLaughlin, Chief Sustainability Officer at Walmart, has been named as number three in Sustainability Magazine’s Top 250 Sustainability Leaders 2026 list.

She has been recognised for her commitment to social responsibility and environmental stewardship while prioritising business growth.

The aviation sector is responsible for approximately 3% of global emissions.

Decarbonising aviation is notoriously difficult, due to the high costs and advanced technologies required for the sector.

Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) could be a solution to these challenges, which can potentially reduce CO₂ emissions by 80% compared to traditional jet fuel.

Airbus is one of the companies working on aviation decarbonisation, with its Chief Sustainability Officer Julie Kitcher leading the company's strategy.

Ahead of her appearance on the Global Decarbonisation Strategies panel at Sustainability LIVE: The Leadership Summit at Climate Week NYC, Julie shares her insights with Sustainability Magazine.

As world and business leaders gather in New York for Climate Action Week, the environmental crisis dominates the global agenda.

The summit follows a year marked by record-breaking heatwaves and devastating wildfires in Africa, compounded by a severe El Niño weather event.

Grounded in unequivocal evidence from NASA that the Earth is warming at an unprecedented rate due to human activity, the call for immediate action has never been more urgent.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband underscored the gravity of the threat, noting that "climate and nature loss represents an urgent national security issue and demands action equal to the scale of the challenge."

Alongside traditional policy debates, a central focus has emerged around the rapid expansion of AI.

The build-out of data centres and soaring demand for computing power have raised deep concerns about AI’s energy and water footprint.

Addressing whether there is good news on the horizon where AI and climate meet, Angela Barranco, Executive Director for North America at Climate Group, convened a high-level panel featuring Dr. Eva Riesenhuber, Global Head of Sustainability at Siemens and Dr. Evelyn Wang, Vice President for Energy and Climate at MIT.

Globally, airlines use an average of 0.8% sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in their fuel mix, but in 2025, Finnair reached 1.6% across its one million tonnes of jet fuel.

Decarbonising aviation relies on expanding SAF use. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), SAF and improved operational efficiency are expected to deliver 65% of the sector’s net-zero emissions reductions by 2050.

Companies are increasingly working together across the value chain to overcome key commercial and supply challenges, instead of relying on piecemeal market deals.

"Finnair and Neste are both Finnish-based companies. Helsinki is Finnair's main hub," said Riku Aho, VP Sustainability at Finnair, at Sustainability LIVE: The London Summit in early September.

"We have worked on sustainable aviation fuel together for more than five years, and for the past three years, we've been more focused on really building safety and literacy around what SAF is and how we can employ and engage the entire value chain, from the fuel producer to the airline to the travelling corporate or the consumer, in order to participate in scaling up SAF as a legitimate solution to decarbonise aviation."

Topline:

President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.

What the White House said: Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including nonprofits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably. A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama.

What the response was: Trump’s move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions.”

What's next: Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The Government Accountability Office says the maneuver, known as a “pocket rescission,” is illegal.

President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.

Trump’s Office of Management and Budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending.”

Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including nonprofits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.

A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama.

Trump’s move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions.”

“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”

Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The Government Accountability Office says the maneuver, known as a “pocket rescission,” is illegal.

Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse.”

Friends & Family Flea, a new market from the team behind Maum Market, will make its debut Saturday in Koreatown.

For organizer Arnold Byun, the launch is something of a homecoming.

Nearly five years ago, Byun and his co-founder, Kioh Park, were living in Koreatown and spending months at Document Coffee Bar dreaming up what would eventually become Maum Market, the Asian makers market they launched in January 2022. The market now has a regular presence at ROW DTLA, where it hosts pop-up markets on Dock Street several times a year.

“The genesis of Maum Market is actually really embedded in Koreatown,” Byun, 31, told The LA Local. “And we have a lot of affection and personal history with Koreatown, so it’s a very personal thing for us just to return to our roots.”

Most of the 24 vendors participating in the first Friends & Family Flea have some connection to Koreatown, Byun said. Some grew up in the neighborhood, some still live there and others have moved away but retain ties to the area. The vendor list includes apparel brands, artists, jewelry makers, beauty and wellness businesses and food vendors.

“We’ve been trying to be pretty intentional about curating from the community as much as possible,” Byun said.

There will be plenty of food and shopping, including “sogeum-bbang,” or salt bread, tea, handmade candles, soaps and vintage clothing, as well as flash tattoos and burgers and fries from Love Hour. The LA Hwatu-Hanafuda Club will teach visitors about hwatu, the Korean deck of playing cards with roots in Japan. The club will also offer $5 tarot card readings.

Eena Cho, founder of the LA Hwatu-Hanafuda Club, was born and raised in Koreatown. She remembers living with her mother in an apartment on Wilshire Boulevard and Vermont Avenue and volunteering at the senior center near Seoul International Park, where she spent time with older Korean residents.

She also grew up playing go-stop with her grandparents during Korean holidays, like Chuseok and Seollal.

“That was a big part of my childhood,” said Cho, 24. “Another part is that living in LA where there’s so many different groups of people together, I remember my best friend Maria growing up, she was Mexican, and we would be playmates because both of our parents were working overtime.”

For Cho, joining Friends & Family Flea felt like a natural fit.

“Koreatown is a beautiful diaspora of many different cultures,” Cho said. “And I think that makes Koreatown, Koreatown.”

The local focus is a big part of what Byun hopes will distinguish Friends & Family from other flea markets and fairs. He said organizers wanted to create something that “intentionally celebrates a specific neighborhood,” in this case, Koreatown.

For the Koreatown market, that also means highlighting small businesses beyond the restaurants that often get the most attention.

“It’s more about, you know, where do we get our dry cleaning, where do we get our shoes done, or these kinds of services that I think don’t get highlighted as often as maybe restaurants do, but are really core and essential parts of a community business,” Byun said.

Byun’s own history with Koreatown also makes the neighborhood an especially fitting place to start.

His family immigrated to the South Bay from Korea in 2002, when he was 6. He remembers coming to Koreatown with his parents on the weekends for Korean meals and grocery trips.

Byun still thinks of the neighborhood as a second home for Korean immigrants, while appreciating how its community has grown more diverse.

“I’m just really happy to see it become a really beloved neighborhood,” he said.

The market is also giving back locally. Hats sold at the event will benefit the Koreatown Youth and Community Center, Byun said.

Friends & Family Flea

Where: Un-Other Space, 524 S. Western Ave., Los Angeles

When: Saturday, Sept. 26, 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Admission is free. Organizers are asking attendees to RSVP.

And this may not be a one-time run. If Saturday goes well, organizers hope to bring Friends & Family Flea back to Koreatown on a monthly basis. They also plan to offer discounted vendor fees to Koreatown residents.

“I feel like there was so much opportunity for us to really hone in and create something more hyperlocal and also really embed ourselves in the community as well,” Byun said.

When I lived in the UK, I worked on a BBC television show about birding. It was a strange experience as I couldn’t exactly book guests — “Hello Mr. Sparrow, could you be on location for an interview at 2 p.m.?”

So instead I spent a lot of time with the crew climbing up mountains with a large tripod on my shoulder. Did you know there’s a bird in the Scottish Highlands whose plumage turns white in winter to blend in with the snow? (It’s called a ptarmigan. Don’t pronounce the p.)

But it did mean I was attuned to British bird calls. I could hear something and pronounce solemnly: “Ah yes, that’s a lark. And that one's a chaffinch."

Moving to LA meant learning a new set of bird calls

When I moved to the U.S., however, it was a whole other story. I really didn’t recognize any of the bird calls. They were all so different. I just shrugged and figured they were part of the backdrop. But one day recently, a woman told me about a free app and said it was life-changing. "Hmm, I’ll see about that," I thought.

Merlin bird app

It’s called Merlin, from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology, and it’s kind of like Shazam for bird calls. As in, you click it, and it tells you what bird song you can hear around you. When I opened it in my backyard for the first time, a whole orchestra of bird sounds opened up around me. I admit: it was kind of life-changing.

Of course it first picked up a crow, which I know only too well, given its loud, raucous sound. But then it identified a house finch. Huh. Who knew they were in my backyard? And as I listened closely, I realized … I knew that sound! It’s the first thing I hear when I wake up at dawn, lovely and melodic.

So now when I open my eyes in the morning, I say, "Good morning, house finch, communing with fellow beings alive on a vibrant California morning!" It kicks off my day, although I guess I’ve been reading too much Mary Oliver.

The backyard birds you're probably hearing right now

But then other birds I didn’t know would pop up on my phone during the day, with names as intriguing as their calls: the spotted towhee, the orange-crowned warbler, or Cassin’s kingbird.

I mean, they do realize they’re in a backyard in Los Angeles, not some estate in Georgian England? My favorite for a while was the dark-eyed junco. Now we’re talking romantic heroes. Imagine him slyly popping across the apple tree limbs to call to you. Dark-Eyed Junco, at your service.

Meet Swinhoe's white-eye, a non-native bird spreading across SoCal

And then there’s Swinhoe’s white-eye. Which sounds a little like an eye ailment, but there you go. It’s a tiny bright yellow bird with a white ring around each eye. So cute! I first noticed them when there were a bazillion of them in a tree outside my house. It was such an unusual sight that I mentioned it to a woman walking her dog, and we stood there, oohing and aahing, until we both realized we’d oohed a little too much, and it was time to go.

When I researched them, I was surprised to find they’re not native to SoCal. They’re actually pretty new to the area. There were just a handful in Orange County 20 years ago, probably having been brought over from Asia as pets and escaped. And now, they’re thriving and have spread everywhere from Baja to San Luis Obispo. Who knows where they’ll end up next? If anyone sees a chartreuse cutie in New York, let me know. It'll probably be very tired.

Yes, you can see I’ve become slightly annoying with my newfound bird interest. I’ll be asking my family what they want for dinner, and I’ll say, “Wait, is that the spotted towhee?” and turn to my phone, and my teenager will wrest it out of my hand and say, “Mom, be in the present!” Which is right. But my morning serenade as the birds come online one by one and greet the new day — well, that’s as present as you can be.

Walk through the automatic doors at the Carson Library and you’ll see on your left a 1973 painting called "Dominoes" by John Riddle.

Riddle, a prominent Black artist, has worked in the L.A. County Museum of Art and the Brooklyn Museum, and has been collected by Jesse Jackson and Roberta Flack.

Riddle's work was previously owned by the Golden State Mutual Life Insurance Company in West Adams. Over two decades, the company’s art director, William Pajaud, an L.A. artist himself, carefully collected hundreds of pieces of Black art. Each piece in the collection, Pajaud said, would be a chapter telling the story of African Americans in the U.S. The collection included oil paintings, watercolors, and sculptures in clay, wood and metal.

When Golden State Mutual Life Insurance shut down, the company sold most of the best pieces at a private auction in 2007, with some selling for hundreds of thousands of dollars. L.A. County was able to acquire about 120 works, including Riddle's piece.

To keep the works accessible to the public and free of charge, county officials chose four public libraries and three community centers to show the work. Earlier this year, the county arts department created a new website with a map to make them easier to find. The locations include the Golden State Mutual historic building in West Adams, plus:

:

Libraries

Carson Library (Carson)

A.C. Bilbrew Library (Willowbrook)

Masao W. Satow Library (Gardena)

View Park Bebe Moore Campbell Library (View Park/Windsor Hills)

Community centers:

Curtis Tucker Behavioral Health Center Health Services (Inglewood)

Willowbrook Senior Center Aging and Disabilities (Willowbrook)

Mark Ridley-Thomas Behavioral Health Center Health Services (on the Martin Luther King, Jr. Medical Campus).

“All of these are county-owned spaces that are available, accessible to the public and to patrons to be able to live with the works, learn about the works, see the works, learn about the works,” said Kristin Sakoda, director of the Los Angeles County Department of Arts and Culture.

As you walk past the checkout desk at the Carson Library, toward the teen section, you’ll see another remarkable piece from the county’s holdings. It’s a two-foot-tall sculpture made from one piece of mahogany. It’s called "The Embrace" by artist Elizabeth Catlett, whose work is in the collection of New York’s Museum of Modern Art, among many other institutions. Catlett depicted two people hugging, their faces and bodies fused together, their eyes looking at the viewer.

In the auction catalogue for the Golden State Collection, Catlett wrote: “I still work figuratively, trying to express emotion through abstract form, color, line, and space. I attempt to reach out to ordinary people who have little or no experience or understanding of art principles, and extend to them what I may feel about a subject."

Meanwhile at A.C. Bilbrew Library, north of Compton, there’s a piece by Charles White, who lived in L.A. County for decades and mentored many artists in the region. His paintings and drawings in the 1960s took on the issues of the Black Civil Rights Movement, and that led well-known Black Americans like Nat King Cole and Eartha Kitt to buy his art.

County officials are hopeful that the communities around these neighborhoods enjoy the art’s benefits, including “mental health, in our education, our youth development, our sense of inclusion and belonging,” Sakoda said.

authors: ANTON L. DELGADO Associated Press, ABC News
description:
UNITED NATIONS -- Addressing the U.N. General Assembly in 2021, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to stop funding overseas coal power plants in an effort to help curb climate change.
But experts have warned that Chinese companies are taking advantage of regulatory loopholes to skirt Xi’s promise and continue investing in overseas coal.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz hit Southeast Asia first and hardest, sending governments into a state of energy triage.

While global coal demand is plateauing, energy-hungry Southeast Asia has been trending in the opposite direction.
text:
UNITED NATIONS -- Addressing the U.N. General Assembly in 2021, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to stop funding overseas coal power plants in an effort to help curb climate change. Five years later, as the assembly meets this week, the world's climate commitments are dangerously offtrack, and the phase down of coal is inching along.

So far, China has canceled the majority of the coal plans it had planned in 2021, according to a new report released this week to align with the General Assembly and New York Climate Week. This is a small bright spot in global efforts to counter climate change, which has driven deadly disasters in Asia in recent months.

But experts have warned that Chinese companies are taking advantage of regulatory loopholes to skirt Xi’s promise and continue investing in overseas coal.

As a key infrastructure funder in the Global South, and as the global leader in electric vehicle, solar panel and wind turbine manufacturing, China is setting the tone for the transition to renewable energy across Asia and Africa. That's why experts have stressed the importance of Beijing's commitment to its 2021 pledge.

Xi skipped the U.N. meeting this week, in favor of a summit with U.S. President Donald Trump, and sent Chinese Vice President Han Zheng to New York instead. Han addresses the General Assembly on Saturday.

Back in 2021, the U.N. climate agency optimistically declared that coal was “consigned to history” after nearly 200 countries agreed to phase down the fossil fuel. But after two energy shocks from the Russia-Ukraine War and the Iran war, the need for “energy security” is altering the future of coal in hard-hit regions, like Southeast Asia.

The energy-hungry region is often referred to as “China’s backyard” and is a major recipient of Chinese funds. The diverse region, which accounts for a fifth of the world's growing energy demand, depended heavily on fossil fuel imports from the Middle East.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz hit Southeast Asia first and hardest, sending governments into a state of energy triage. Multiple nations have ramped up coal use to survive the crisis, which has also signaled to governments the need for renewable energy. Regional nations are investing in rooftop solar, incentivizing electric vehicles and exploring nuclear power.

While renewable energy is expanding quickly, coal remains indispensable in Asia.

“The growing desire among countries in Southeast Asia to secure reliable energy supplies could bring about another round of coal fever,” said Li Shuo, director of the Asia Society Policy Institute’s China Climate Hub, which “will continue to test the resolve behind the coal moratorium.”

China was the world’s largest overseas coal financier until Xi made his 2021 promise.

“This marked the first time Beijing was willing to extend its emerging climate ambition beyond its borders,” Li said.

China is currently the world's largest annual emitter of carbon dioxide, though the U.S. is the largest historic emitter globally.

While China's coal use is slowly decreasing, it still leads the world in building out new domestic coal infrastructure. Coal has been China's ubiquitous energy source for decades; when China re-opened to the U.S. in 1979, arriving Americans disembarked into cities that smelled heavily of burning coal, whose residue quickly gathered on clothes and skin.

Now, China dominates the global electric vehicle market and is the world's largest solar panel and wind turbine producer — consistently setting records for massive rollouts of renewable energy.

“The rapid expansion of clean energy, both in China and increasingly abroad, since the announcement of the coal moratorium should encourage Beijing to further prioritize renewable energy in its international energy strategy," Li said.

China has cancelled 67% of the coal power capacity it had planned to build overseas in 2021, according to a new report by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, and the People of Asia for Climate Solutions, or PACS.

By cancelling these projects — totaling 61.5 gigawatts — China avoided 6.4 billion tons of lifetime carbon dioxide emissions, the report estimates.

China somewhat delivering on its 2021 pledge is a positive story, said Syahdiva Moezbar, an industry analyst with CREA in the Indonesian capital of Jakarta, but “coal expansion hasn’t stopped because of the nature of the pledge itself, which still allows private Chinese companies to invest overseas.”

Indonesia has seen a boom in coal plants funded by Chinese companies to specifically power heavy industries, like the smelting of nickel and aluminum, without linking to the national power grid. This is known as “captive coal."

Indonesia takes the top spot for continued Chinese investments, with 17.1 gigawatts of China-backed coal capacity planned. Vietnam and Pakistan are a far second and third with less than 4 gigawatts in the works, the report found.

“When commercial interests take precedence over China’s broader green development commitments and the world’s climate security, the benefits of China’s remarkable clean-energy leadership are undermined,” said Xiaojun Wang, PACS' executive director, in a statement with the report.

This has been complicated further by the Iran war energy shock which is a harsh wake-up call for Southeast Asia. The Philippines, Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam all ramped up coal use because of the Iran war.

While global coal demand is plateauing, energy-hungry Southeast Asia has been trending in the opposite direction.

Southeast Asia accounts for nearly 20% of global energy demand growth through 2035, according to the International Energy Agency, which stated that the “crisis is prompting a reassessment of policy and investment strategies amid a strong prioritization of energy security.”

The energy transition is “a two-party tango,” said Li of the China Climate Hub, stressing that both China and its partner must be equally committed to phasing down coal. While it's been five years since the pledge, he said, “this saga is far from over.”

FIRST ON FOX: American households could end up paying $1,465 more per year on average in energy costs if "anti-energy" climate lawsuits against oil and gas companies are successful, according to a new report first obtained by Fox News Digital.

Americans will "pay a lot more" if the far-left "get their way," warned Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J Antoni, who co-authored the report with Power The Future founder Daniel Turner.

Hundreds of lawsuits and other state-level "climate superfund" laws could increase the cost of gasoline, electricity and other everyday necessities Americans rely on, the report estimates.

SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA

The new analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear a closely-watched lawsuit next month out of Boulder, Colorado, which could drastically shape the future of climate litigation.

"If those folks on the radical left wing who are anti-energy, if they get their way, your costs are going to go up," Antoni told Fox News Digital. "Your household is going to pay a lot more. The energy is going to get much more expensive."

"You may think it's bad now, but it will get significantly worse," he added.

The report estimates energy companies could face an additional $194 billion in annual costs, which the authors argue would ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices rather than absorbed entirely by companies or their shareholders.

Those costs could add roughly 41 cents to a gallon of gasoline and increase residential electricity rates by about 8.6%, according to the analysis.

"Every single time a company is sued, yes, they pay some damages, but ultimately they will just charge people more for their product to recoup those losses," Turner told Fox News Digital.

LAWSUITS COST EVERY AMERICAN HOUSEHOLD THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS. SUPREME COURT CAN HELP

The report examined more than 300 pending lawsuits, three state "climate superfund" laws, 12 state legislative proposals and one federal bill. Its estimate reflects a "full-success scenario" in which all of those measures prevail; it does not predict that they will.

The analysis counted each lawsuit only once and excluded duplicate filings. In fact, Antoni said the estimate may be conservative because some lawsuits do not specify the damages they are seeking, leaving potential court awards open-ended.

The legal efforts include New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act, which was blocked by a federal judge in August, and the Supreme Court’s pending Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County case.

That case could determine whether state and local governments can pursue climate lawsuits against fossil fuel companies in state court.

GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'HIDDEN CLIMATE TAX' HITTING AMERICANS NATIONWIDE, LAWMAKER WARNS

Turner argued the lawsuits could also shift responsibility away from state and local leaders.

"The concern about these superfund lawsuits is that they absolve elected leaders from doing the bad, boring part of governing, which is infrastructure and mitigation strategies," he said.

Despite the rise in climate lawsuits and state "superfund" laws, Antoni said the issue has largely flown under the radar.

text:
A planned Amazon data center is facing a challenge to its intention to use nearly 650 diesel generators as temporary and backup power.

The Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of a local activist group in Richmond County, has asked state officials to host another hearing about two air quality permits that were recently awarded to Amazon and Duke Energy for the diesel generators.

Amazon plans to build the data center right next to Duke Energy’s natural gas power plant in Richmond County. Amazon recently secured an air quality permit to operate 588 diesel generators as backup power, which would be used in case of a power outage.

Duke Energy got a separate air quality permit to operate another 57 diesel generators, which it will use to temporarily power the data center for its first several months of operation before it’s fully connected to Duke’s electric grid.

Richmond County residents have criticized the project, saying the diesel generators will increase air pollution in a community that’s already facing poor air quality and above-average rates of respiratory health problems.

In two petitions filed to the North Carolina Office of Administrative Hearings on Friday, the SELC said that, by splitting the 600-plus diesel generators into two separate air quality permits, Duke and Amazon are “illegally evading requirements of the Clean Air Act,” and downplaying the level of pollutants that the entire project will emit.

The petitions argue that state officials made a mistake when they issued the air quality permits, and asks the state to revoke the permits.

“In our community already exposed to multiple air pollution sources and struggling for access to healthcare, what happens to people when one of the world’s wealthiest companies spews even more harmful pollution from 649 diesel-fired generators for its data center?” said Shaun Ingram, co-founder of the Richmond County Coalition for Justice and Black Empowerment, in a Friday news release.

State officials have said that Duke and Amazon’s air quality permits should be reviewed separately because Duke’s diesel generators will not be running at the same time as Amazon’s. The 57 diesel generators sought by Duke will only power the data center until it’s fully connected to the electric grid, and the 588 diesel generators sought by Amazon will serve as backup power after the project connects to the grid.

When issuing the air quality permits last month, officials also said the two companies’ permits should be separate because they “are not under the control of the same company and the two permits serve different purposes on different time horizons.”

However, the SELC reviewed a contract between Duke and Amazon that would give Amazon some control over when Duke’s diesel generators operate, according to their petition. Attorney Caroline Cress argued that that contract means they should be considered as part of the same project.
