text:
Power Electronics a global company specializing in solutions for solar energy, storage, data centers, e-mobility, and drives, celebrated the groundbreaking of its future campus in Houston, Texas, marking a major milestone in the company’s long-term growth and industrial strategy in the United States.

The ceremony brought together Power Electronics’ executive leadership, government officials and authorities, customers, industry partners and members of the Houston business community to recognize the beginning of a new chapter in the company’s U.S. operations.

Located on more than 53 acres, the new campus represents a significant expansion of Power Electronics’ manufacturing footprint in the United States. The project will include two buildings of approximately 150,000 and 700,000 square feet, bringing together Logistics, Production, Electronics Manufacturing, R&D, Training, Corporate Offices, and other key functions within a single industrial campus.

Once fully operational, the Houston campus is expected to deliver up to 40 GW of annual production capacity and create over 400 new jobs in the Houston area.

Designed to become Power Electronics’ most automated inverter production site to date, the campus will incorporate advanced production technologies and processes focused on efficiency, quality, scalability and reliability.

Strengthening U.S. Energy Infrastructure Through Local Manufacturing

The new Houston campus comes at a critical time for the U.S. energy industry, as accelerating demand from utility-scale solar, storage, data centers and broader electrification continues to increase the need for reliable power conversion solutions and resilient domestic supply chains.

The Houston campus represents more than additional production capacity. It is a long-term investment in American industry, skilled employment, technological innovation and the infrastructure required to support the next generation of the U.S. energy system.

“For the first time in many years, the United States will be able to meet its growing need for sustainable power generation capacity and energy resilience through local manufacturing, supported by the most advanced technology in the world. Our 40 GW Houston Campus will help shape the future of energy and AI growth globally,” said David Salvo, CEO of Power Electronics.

Built on Decades of Power Electronics Expertise

With 40 years of experience and more than 116 GW installed in the U.S., Power Electronics has built its position as a global industry leader through a continued focus on innovation, advanced manufacturing and service.

The United States has become a key market in the company’s global strategy. For more than a decade, Power Electronics has steadily strengthened its presence across the country, building local teams, operations and technical expertise to serve some of the most significant and demanding energy projects in the U.S.

By continuing to invest in manufacturing, engineering, talent and service resources, Power Electronics is reinforcing its long-term commitment to the market and its role in advancing the infrastructure needed for the next generation of energy development. With the addition of the Houston campus, Power Electronics will further strengthen its global manufacturing platform and reach up to 105 GW of annual production capacity worldwide, combining its operations in the United States and Europe to support customers with greater scale, proximity and resilience across key energy markets.

text:
Litigation over the EPA’s rollback of Biden-era power plant emission rules will likely put the Trump administration in the position of poking holes in a technology it has, at other times, incentivized and promoted.

The dispute over carbon capture and sequestration could also rehash highly technical, often speculative financial arguments that have been tabled before — except this time with the government arguing the technology isn’t economically feasible, rather than that it is, as the Biden administration did.

The Environmental Protection Agency’s recent final rule unwinds a 2024 standard that required coal and new natural gas-fired power plants to dramatically cut their carbon emissions. Under the 2024 rule, the agency said carbon capture and sequestration — capturing and storing releases from burning coal rather than letting them escape into the air — was the best technology for plants to reduce emissions.

But carbon capture doesn’t meet the Clean Air Act’s definition of “best system of emissions reduction,” which requires that a technology be both effective at cutting emissions and available at a cost that doesn’t bring on extreme economic hardship, said Matthew Leopold, who served as EPA general counsel in the first Trump administration.

“The idea that every coal plant in America could bolt on CCS like you would a scrubber — that’s not the case,” Leopold, now a partner at Holland & Knight LLP, said in an interview. “So the Biden EPA’s version of the rule failed to comply with the legal standard, that there’s technology that exists that’s been adequately demonstrated and is cost effective.”

In her dissent in West Virginia v. EPA, in which the Supreme Court found the agency can’t compel a nationwide pivot away from fossil fuels, Justice Elena Kagan conceded that the Clean Air Act compels the agency to “take account of both costs and varied ‘nonair’ impacts (on health, the environment, and the supply of energy).”

Leopold’s view matches President Donald Trump’s EPA, which said in the new rule that a system that captures 90% of the carbon dioxide from a power plant — the level laid out by the Biden rule — hasn’t been adequately demonstrated, and its costs are “not reasonable.”

Moreover, a large network of pipelines and sequestration facilities would have to be built, and that’s unlikely to happen before the Jan. 1, 2032 compliance date established by the Biden rule, the EPA said.

Prior Support

But even as the EPA has queried the feasibility of carbon capture, the Trump administration has supported it.

Trump’s 2025 tax and spending law expanded the section 45Q tax credit, which offers subsidies of $85 to $180 per ton for companies that capture and store carbon dioxide.

Some states and Congressional lawmakers have said that move has been undermined by the EPA’s cancellation of the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, the mechanism the federal government uses to confirm that carbon is being stored.

The EPA has also tried to clear the backlog of applications for underground CO2 injection wells — the last stage of the carbon capture process — by allowing states like Texas and West Virginia to make permitting decisions.

“This administration first insisted that any power plant pollution rules could use only on-site pollution controls,” said Trevor Higgins, senior vice president of energy and environment at the Center for American Progress. “Now they insist that there are no on-site pollution controls that are worth the expense when ignoring the value of the human lives it would save.”

Despite its occasional support, the Trump administration’s decision to point to carbon capture as unfeasible in its justification for revoking the Biden rule is poised to be scrutinized.

The Natural Resources Defense Council and Clean Air Task Force on Sept. 17 asked the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit to review the Trump administration’s rule.

Both groups say the Trump rule uses flawed math and iffy assumptions to calculate costs, and even then still shows 90% carbon capture to be available at a reasonable cost, according to comments filed last year.

Flawed Math?

The EPA’s calculations include a capacity factor assumption that flies in the face of the evidence, an incorrect suggestion on whether tax credits should be included in cost analyses, the “complete disregard” of the benefits of addressing climate change, and an arbitrary comparison to previous findings about how reasonable the costs are, the groups wrote.

The Biden EPA amassed an extensive scientific and technical record supporting the feasibility of carbon capture, examining technology installed at plants across the world, Meredith Hankins, federal climate legal director at NRDC, said in an interview before her organization filed its petition for review.

That review included close scrutiny of the feasibility and affordability questions, Hankins said.

“It’s not like these rules were requiring every single power plant in the country to install CCS,” Hankins said. “They were actually quite reasonable; the standards for coal plants were designed around expected retirement dates. So if a plant was expected to retire before 2039, they didn’t have to install CCS.”

Some of the cost arguments that may arise in court rest on speculative financial forecasts about how power plant operators will behave in response to different incentives. The NRDC and Clean Air Task Force comments claim that once a plant goes to the expense of installing carbon capture, it will have a financial incentive to use it as much as possible.

“This situation may be an example of being careful what you ask for,” said Steve Solow, former chief of the Justice Department’s environmental crime section.

The Trump White House has supported the ending of Chevron deference when it disagrees with prior administrations’ interpretations of what the law requires, but by the same token, courts no longer have to give deference to the current EPA’s interpretation either, said Solow, now an environmental law professor at Pace University’s environmental law program.

“Instead, the administration will have to convince a judge that the administration’s view is the best reading of what the law requires, and not just a permissible one,” he said.

text:
See whether e-bikes qualify for a federal tax credit in 2026, how local rebates differ, and what to verify before counting an incentive.

As of July 30, 2026, there is no enacted nationwide federal tax credit for an ordinary consumer purchase of an electric bike in the United States.

State and local e-bike rebate programs may still be available, but they often have limited funding, income requirements, advance-application rules, approved retailers, or eligible-bike lists. A program covered in the news may already have exhausted its funding or formally ended.

That makes the most dangerous line in a purchase budget not the price of the bike, but an incentive being treated as cash before it has been approved.

The Federal Clean Vehicle Credit Does Not Apply to an Ordinary E-bike

Electric bikes are sometimes confused with electric vehicles that qualify for a clean vehicle credit. The IRS instructions for Form 8936 cover qualified clean vehicles and base the relevant vehicle definitions on requirements that include at least four wheels. A two- or three-wheeled electric bike does not enter the automobile tax-credit program simply because it has a battery and motor.

Current IRS information also states that the relevant clean vehicle credits no longer apply to vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025. Even without that cutoff date, an ordinary e-bike does not meet the basic requirement of having at least four wheels.

Seeing an "electric vehicle" option in tax software does not make the purchase price of an electric bike eligible. Tax treatment requires a clear basis in law and should not be inferred from a product name.

A Proposed E-bike Credit in Congress Is Not Yet Claimable

As of July 30, 2026, H.R. 6900 contains a proposed electric bicycle tax credit, but Congress.gov lists its status as Introduced and shows that it has been referred to committee.

Introduced means a bill has been submitted. It does not mean the bill has passed the House and Senate or been signed by the president. A proposed credit percentage, price cap, or eligibility rule in the bill cannot be used as current tax law.

When a future headline says that the "federal e-bike tax credit is back," check four items on Congress.gov: the current status, the date of the latest action, whether both chambers have passed it, and whether it has become Public Law. A lawmaker's proposal or a news story alone still does not make the credit available.

Rebates, Tax Credits, and Store Discounts Are Not the Same

Type of savings When it is received What is most often misunderstood Tax credit Usually claimed when filing a tax return under applicable law It may not have the same practical value for every taxpayer, and a product name alone does not establish eligibility Point-of-sale rebate Deducted at purchase or redeemed with a voucher Advance approval may be required, with limits on retailers, models, income, or residency Post-purchase rebate Paid after the buyer submits documents for a completed purchase Deadlines, funding limits, and the possibility of denial may apply Utility/employer benefit Provided by a utility, local organization, or employer Coverage and eligibility are narrow, and the rules may change Brand discount Provided by the seller as a coupon or price reduction It is not a government incentive and generally does not create tax eligibility

A product page that says "save $100" is not the same as government approval for a 100-dollar rebate. The first is used under the seller's terms; the second must be confirmed through the government or organization running the program.

The Biggest Problem With Local Rebates Is That Their Status Changes

Why Are Old Incentive Articles So Easy to Misread?

E-bike incentives often operate with limited funding. An old program page remaining online does not mean applications are still open.

For example, the California Air Resources Board's California E-Bike Incentive Project page states that the program ended in December 2025. The MassCEC e-bike program page also shows that its 2025 program has closed and is not expected to reopen in 2026.

Both programs were real, but neither is proof that an incentive remains available for a purchase in 2026. An old news article, a retailer's archived campaign page, or a social media screenshot may help identify a program by name. Its official page must provide the final word on current status.

Check These Seven Things When a Local Program Appears

Is the application open? The page should show a current funding round, opening date, or waitlist rather than only describing a past program.

Must the application come first? Many programs require an approved voucher before purchase. Ordering early can make the purchase ineligible.

What are the residency and income rules? A city, county, or state boundary, an income threshold, or participation in a particular public-assistance program may affect eligibility.

What bikes qualify? Class, maximum price, motor power, certification, new-bike status, and a separate allowance for cargo e-bikes may all matter.

Which retailers qualify? An online purchase, an out-of-state seller, or a bike shop outside the partner network may not be accepted.

Is funding still available? An active program does not necessarily have money remaining. Some programs distribute funds on a first-come basis or through a lottery.

Can the incentive be combined with other savings? Brand discounts, local rebates, employer benefits, and sales-tax rules may conflict.

Without a written answer from the program, a salesperson's "it should qualify" should not enter the household budget.

Can KODA Qualify for an Incentive?

Whether the Letrigo KODA electric cargo bike qualifies for a local program depends entirely on that program's current rules. Its status as a cargo e-bike and relevant certifications for the complete bike or battery may satisfy requirements in some programs, but they do not create nationwide eligibility.

Before ordering, compare KODA's class, rated motor power, price, certifications, purchase channel, and retailer information with the program's checklist. Obtain the voucher or written approval first. If a program requires an approved retailer, the transaction channel may affect eligibility even when the same model is available from the brand's website.

The same rule applies when comparing other electric cargo bikes: do not rank them first by an expected price after an unapproved incentive. Compare the actual price the household can afford, then treat an approved incentive as an additional reduction.

No Approval Number Means the Decision Should Use the Full Price

As of July 30, 2026, an ordinary electric bike does not have a nationwide federal purchase tax credit that consumers can simply claim, and a proposal in Congress is still not current law. Each local rebate requires a check of the official program page, application order, personal eligibility, bike requirements, and retailer rules.

When buying Letrigo e-bikes or another brand, first decide whether the full price is affordable without an incentive. Add the savings to the final budget only after receiving a valid voucher, approval notice, or clear written confirmation of eligibility.

That is not excessive caution. It prevents a program intended to lower the cost from creating a budget shortfall instead.

Dive Brief:

A U.S. District Court judge for the District of Columbia on Tuesday ruled that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency illegally terminated the $7 billion Solar for All program in a lawsuit brought by Harris County, Texas, last October.

The decision comes less than a week after the U.S. District Court of Rhode Island on Friday ruled the EPA’s termination of the Solar for All program was procedurally unlawful in a lawsuit filed on behalf of downstream beneficiaries of Solar for All grants.

The EPA is reviewing both decisions and considering options for appeal, it said in emails to Smart Cities Dive. A third lawsuit contending the grant cancellation was illegal, filed by 22 states and the District of Columbia in U.S. District Court in the Western District of Washington last October, was dismissed in January.

Dive Insight:

The Texas Solar for All Coalition was awarded nearly $250 million in 2024 to expand solar access across the state as part of the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund established by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. Harris County — the state’s largest county and home to Houston — led the coalition and secured more than $54 million.

The EPA eliminated the program in August 2025, citing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but the lawsuit states “the OBBBA provides no authority for EPA’s Elimination Decision.”

District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan wrote in her Sept. 22 ruling that EPA’s decision to eliminate the Solar for All program without congressional authorization was “arbitrary and capricious, contrary to law, and in excess of statutory authority.”

That decision applies to the EPA’s cancellation of all Solar for All grants, not just Harris County’s, Chutkan ruled. “What the court sets aside is the agency’s policy-level determination that OBBA rendered continued operation of SFA legally impermissible — [which is] applicable to the program as a whole,” she wrote.

The EPA’s termination of Harris County’s Solar for All grant and the resulting legal fight have set the county back in building clean energy initiatives to help low-income households save on energy costs, create jobs and establish solar-powered community hubs for the county to use in the event of power outages and state grid failures, according to a Harris County news release.

“This is a really important victory for energy resilience in Harris County,” Harris County Judge Lina Hidalgo said in a statement Wednesday. “The fight continues but this is a big step to getting our funding back.”

title: The charge is on for more EV chargers - WardsAuto
description:
He used an app to learn where regional public chargers were.
Even though EV vehicle sales are in a slump (largely due to the end of federal tax credits last year), public EV charger installations are on a hitting streak.
It may seem counterintuitive to install more public chargers when EV deliveries are soft.
While many EV buyers install home chargers — typically a 240V Level 2 — apartment dwellers and others often lack on-premises charger access.
“Even if we had more EV chargers, consumers won’t flock to EVs at their current price points,” he told me.
text:
Nine years ago, Bob Gritzinger drove a Chevrolet Bolt EV from his home outside Detroit to Traverse City, Michigan, about 230 miles away. It became an EV road-trip challenge. An ice cream shop saved the day.

His car’s battery range was short of his destination. So, he needed to recharge a bit somewhere. He used an app to learn where regional public chargers were. But the app didn’t say which ones worked.

Many didn’t, as Gritzinger, a former WardsAuto colleague of mine, discovered.

But he found a spot with a functioning Level 2 charger. Of all places, it was at a Dairy Queen in Grayling, Michigan.

“The cord was lying in the grass behind the building, but it worked,” said Gritzinger. “I had a hamburger and milk shake while waiting.”

That was then. Today the public charging network is much better, if not perfect, but there are a number of charging-station choices on the way to Traverse City.

Even though EV vehicle sales are in a slump (largely due to the end of federal tax credits last year), public EV charger installations are on a hitting streak. That’s because of an ambitious industry push to install more public chargers in the U.S.

As of August, according to the Alternative Fuels Data Center, the U.S. had more than 80,000 public EV charging station locations and over 250,000 individual charging ports. Thousands of new ports are being added each quarter.

It may seem counterintuitive to install more public chargers when EV deliveries are soft. But many in the industry say more chargers will yield more EV sales.

After all, car shoppers’ main reason for passing on buying an EV is charger availability, according to JD Power.

While many EV buyers install home chargers — typically a 240V Level 2 — apartment dwellers and others often lack on-premises charger access. Public charging is for them. It’s also a must for road trippers.

“We need to grow the public-charging infrastructure so consumers feel confident,” Brent Gruber, JD Power’s executive director of EV solutions, told me.

The type of charger matters too, as there are three types of chargers:

Level 1 uses a standard 120V household outlet. That provides roughly 3 to 5 miles of range per hour. So, sit back, relax and maybe crack open a copy of “War and Peace” while waiting.

Level 2 ups the voltage to 240V, the kind that powers home washers and dryers. It provides 25–40 miles of range per hour — or, perhaps, a full charge overnight.

Level 3 direct current (DC) can do the job in less than an hour.

Building America’s public charging infrastructure remains a work in progress, but across the industry, coalitions to expand charging availability continue to be formed.

“The flywheel is in motion,” Will Hotchkiss, head of public charging at General Motors, told me at a charging station opening in Michigan in August, which coincided with an an Automotive Press Association event. But like any technology, Hotchkiss added, “there’s always a ramp curve.”

The event was to celebrate a new EVgo station opening at a Meijer, and built in partnership with GM. The charging station is considered a “flagship” location for EVgo because of its high-power chargers, size, and its access to amenities like shopping, dining and grocery while charging occurs.

Featured at one end of the Meijer parking lot were EVgo’s latest high-speed chargers, increasing the number of charging stalls there from five to 15.

More chargers will help — but vehicle cost needs to come down

EVgo CEO Badar Kahn said at the event his company plans to add thousands more stalls by 2030.

But will more public charging stations spur EV sales?

“Absolutely,” he responded. “Two top-of-mind considerations for people thinking about buying an EV are the price of the vehicle and where to charge it.”

While the charging part is important, most people who consider buying an EV but ultimately don’t, cite the sticker price as the No.1 reason, said Kevin Roberts, director of economic and market intelligence for CarGurus, an online automotive marketplace.

“Even if we had more EV chargers, consumers won’t flock to EVs at their current price points,” he told me. “Consumers are looking for more affordable options.”

Hybrid vehicles with combined gasoline-electric propulsion systems have become a popular alternative to all-electric.

“We’re starting to see the demand that everyone expected for non-internal combustion engines, but one of the biggest headwinds facing EVs now is that consumers really seem to like hybrids,” Roberts said.

User satisfaction has rated highest for DC chargers at hotels, gas stations/convenience stores and restaurants, while car dealerships score significantly lower, according to JD Power polling.

Andrew DiFeo, general manager of Hyundai of St. Augustine in Florida said his dealership has onsite Level 2 and 3 chargers. But people aren’t lined up to use them.

“It’s pretty much a convenience for customers, however our charging station isn’t something I think about daily.”

Yet is a well-functioning, widespread fast-charging network necessary for an EV breakout?

“I would say yes,” said DiFeo. “The charging infrastructure has to be there for mass adoption of EVs, whatever percentage that will be,”

Read More in Automakers

Right now, it’s tough for automakers to try to figure out how many EVs to build — and when — as that market fluctuates, he noted. “I don’t envy manufacturers who must go back and forth with production to meet where demand is. It’s tricky, pricey and time-consuming.”

text:
The Canada Investment Summit, which concluded on Sept. 15, outlined the federal government’s plan to catalyze $1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years.

The event brought together global investors managing more than $100 trillion in assets who have already committed nearly $500 billion in new investment to Canada.

In his keynote address, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced several major policy measures: a new productivity mega deduction for business investment, a streamlined permission process for new projects, a formal asset-recycling policy and plans to seek private investment for Canada’s four largest airports.

Investors attending the summit were also presented with a pitch book featuring 167 potential projects across sectors including energy, mining, infrastructure, manufacturing and technology.

These announcements signal a change in Canada’s economic strategy: using public policy to attract private capital at a much larger scale and across more sectors.

Incentivizing private investment

The first group of announcements focuses on reducing barriers to investment, including the cost of capital investment, regulatory uncertainty and the challenge of identifying viable projects.

The most significant is the new Productivity Mega Deduction, which allows businesses to write off most new capital investments immediately, effectively lowering the marginal tax rate on new investment from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent.

The government estimates the measure could increase economic output by $22 billion annually and raise long-term employment by up to 80,000 jobs. However, it is also expected to cost the government $36 billion in lost revenue over the next five years.

If the projected benefits do not materialize in new projects that would not have otherwise occurred, budget deficits could increase, leaving taxpayers to ultimately foot the bill.

The mega deduction also expands the types of investments eligible for immediate tax write-offs compared with the previous Productivity Super-Deduction. While the earlier policy focused more on areas like clean energy, data network infrastructure and scientific research, the new approach expands eligibility to include controversial areas such as oil and gas pipelines and commercial aircraft.

Faster approvals for major projects

The second investment incentive involves speeding up project approvals. The federal government has promised a new standard of “one project, one review, one year,” arguing that faster permitting would lower the barrier to new investment.

Lengthy and uncertain approval processes have been identified by businesses as a barrier to investment, particularly for major infrastructure, energy and natural resource projects that can require years of regulatory review before construction begins.

However, accelerating approvals involves balancing competing objectives. It remains unclear how this policy will co-exist alongside provincial permitting processes, and whether accelerated timelines could undermine regulation aimed at protecting Indigenous rights and ecosystems.

Building an investment pipeline

The third incentive relates to the pitch book of 167 projects, which is intended to lower search costs and reduce information barriers for investors considering opportunities in Canada.

The document includes projects from clean energy (31 projects totalling approximately $94 billion) and conventional energy (11 projects totalling $108 billion), as well as marine infrastructure, mining, utilities, transportation, digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing.

It remains unclear how many of these projects — which Energy Minister Tim Hodgson called “conversation starters” — will ultimately proceed, nor how they relate to other government commitments, such as the Paris Agreement.

Among eight projects in New Brunswick listed in the pitch book, for instance, only one has received conditional environmental approval.

Private investment in airports

One of the most prominent announcements from the summit was the government’s plan to seek private investment through long-term concessions for the operation of Canada’s four largest airports: Toronto Pearson, Montréal-Trudeau, Vancouver International and Calgary International.

The federal government says it will retain ownership of the land and underlying assets while selling the rights to private investors to operate the airports in order to provide capital for future infrastructure projects. Airports are currently operated by private, not-for-profit airport authorities.

The initiative builds on the government’s broader “asset optimization” or “asset recycling” approach, under which existing public assets can be used to attract private capital that is then redirected toward new infrastructure.

Existing research on airport privatization has highlighted increased cost with poorer service, with significantly different outcomes depending on the type of privatized ownership.

A recent study covering 437 airport privatizations over 25 years found that, while privatization does not improve airport performance on average, private equity ownership leads to strong and persistent improvements in higher traffic volume, better efficiency, increased access to low-cost carriers and reduced cancellation rates.

A broader economic bet

Compared to past government initiatives, the Canada Investment Summit signals a broader approach focused on attracting investment across a range of sectors rather than targeting only areas of strategic interest.

Previous federal investment strategies have often focused on specific priorities, including clean technology, electric vehicles and critical minerals through targeted tax credits, funds and industrial programs.

This new approach may serve to draw in more investment than the existing, targeted incentives, perhaps increasing economic growth and creating new jobs. At the same time, broad-based incentives raise questions about the type of economy being built and the distribution of benefits and costs.

As protesters at the summit highlighted, many of the proposed investments involve the oil and gas sector or projects that may affect Indigenous territories.

There are serious questions remaining about who will profit from this broad-based strategy, and who will be negatively impacted, especially given concerns about the economic impacts of government incentives on the federal government’s finances and the potential environmental consequences of some projects.

title: Why farmers are pairing crops with solar panels - DW News
description:
Letting sheep roam under solar panels is just one of many forms of a burgeoning strategy called agrivoltaics, where crops grow or livestock graze in tandem with renewable energy infrastructure.
The panels can also protect crops from the elements as well as divert water to them, creating cooler, damper conditions that even boost yields.

In Europe, if agrivoltaics were implemented on just 1% of available agricultural land, the continent could exceed its solar energy targets for 2030.

text:
Traditionally, solar panel farms are quiet — save for the faint hum of the inverter. But on about one in 10 of American solar farms, there's a new sound reverberating through fields: baaaa.

Letting sheep roam under solar panels is just one of many forms of a burgeoning strategy called agrivoltaics, where crops grow or livestock graze in tandem with renewable energy infrastructure.

It's not only of potential benefit for the animals, which get additional shade. The panels can also protect crops from the elements as well as divert water to them, creating cooler, damper conditions that even boost yields.

And even the solar panels themselves tend to respond well to this co-existence — as the cooler they are, the more electricity they produce per watt of sunlight.

"Having concrete or something underneath the solar panels — you're going to have lower efficiency than having something like plants that are transpiring and cooling off on the land surface," Carl Bernacchi, professor of plant biology and crop sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told DW.

While the potential is enormous, especially as climate change puts more and more heat stress on agriculture, the practice is still in its infancy. In Europe, if agrivoltaics were implemented on just 1% of available agricultural land, the continent could exceed its solar energy targets for 2030.

But uptake has been slow: agrivoltaics represents just 18.4 gigawatts of energy worldwide as of mid-2025, less than 1% of the world's solar capacity.

What thrives under the panels

The idea for agrivoltaics dates back to 1981, when two German scientists published an article titled "Kartoffeln unter dem Kollektor" (or "Potatoes beneath the collector"). But the first pilot project didn't begin until 2004 in Japan, a land-constrained country, where there's particular concern over balancing solar deployment with the protection of farmland.

There are three main types of agrivoltaics: horizontal, where panels look directly up at the sky, vertical, where they're placed in large rows, perpendicular to the ground, and integrated, often installed atop greenhouses.

Research suggests shade-tolerant crops stand to benefit. That includes berries, grapes and tomatoes — where the panels' steel framing often doubles as trellises — as well as peaches and peppers.

The panels can also prevent water from fully evaporating, creating a more humid microclimate that benefits the soil — though humidity is a double-edged sword, sometimes introducing plant disease.

Sheep have also proven to be a particularly good match. Compared to cattle or goats, they're generally easier to manage around solar infrastructure, less likely to damage equipment, and small enough to fit comfortably beneath panels. The practice has other sustainability upsides too: sheep manure fertilizes the soil, and sites require less herbicide.

"If we look at the sheep industry, this has been a real paradigm shift for them, where instead of having to pay to lease land to graze their animals — now they're actually getting paid to graze," said Austin Kinzer, an agrivoltaics specialist at the American Farmland Trust conservation movement . "So it completely puts the economics on its head and is a huge opportunity for the sheep industry, which is really struggling in the US pretty much since World War II."

A double climate win

Agrivoltaics sit at a rare intersection of climate mitigation (cutting emissions) and adaptation (adjusting to a warming planet).

"It is both, which is pretty unique as far as climate solutions go," Kinzer said.

The practice offers one answer to where solar panels could go, helping to produce cheaper and more efficient energy, while also benefiting crops that might struggle due to rising temperatures or volatile weather.

And research suggests that climate change will only make regions grow drier, "broadening areas where agrivoltaics can mitigate crop yield penalties (even boosting yield) and improve overall profitability," writeresearchers in a journal article for Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).

A dual-income stream can also offer farmers some insurance should temperature or weather knock out a season's plantings.

"Being able to have that alternate form of income, it's massive for folks who are depending on weather to make their living that is becoming increasingly more extreme and varied," Kinzer said.

Not every farm benefits

So why has adoption been so slow?

"In theory, it's a win-win scenario," Bernacchi said. "But of course, with any technologies, there are always caveats and issues."

One reason is that agrivoltaics don't work everywhere. In America's arid West, where heat stress and less available water can threaten crops, yields stayed the same or even rose under panels. In the humid Midwest, on the other hand, panel shading limited photosynthesis and led to reduced yields in maize and soybeans.

For cash crops, where there's a very small margin for profit, even a minor reduction in yield is a no-go for many farmers.

Then there's the expense. For solar producers, every added inch to mount panels higher means more labor and steel costs. And farmers might need to find new equipment or change methods to adapt to a new system.

"Farmers want to learn from other farmers," said Kinzer, who works with farmers across the US to see how agrivoltaics are being adopted. "They want to hear from folks who are doing it. And so there's a little bit of a chicken-and-the-egg problem for farmers: In most cases, they can't just go across the street or into the next county over and see a project like this and talk to the farmers doing it."

Bridging the divide between farmers and solar

Solar power's land footprint has made it controversial in certain communities — some farming associations have protested converting farmland into acres of solar panels, arguing their members cease to be farmers and become energy producers instead.

It's a tension agrivoltaics helps to address.

One survey found that more than 80% of Americans would be more likely to support solar development in their community, if it allowed for the co-production of energy and agriculture — about 10% more than those that support solar development in general.

"There's this cultural conflict between the farmers who want to farm and the solar companies that want to produce electricity," Bernacchi said. "And agrivoltaics really does bill itself as sort of a middle ground. You can still farm and still get the electricity from the same land."

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — In a brand-new episode of the Republican Study Committee’s (RSC) Right to the Point podcast, Rep. Pete Stauber (MN-08), sits down with Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04), Chairman of the House Committee on Natural Resources, to discuss the urgent need for permitting reform to achieve American energy independence, bring more jobs back to America, and bolster national security.

The Congressmen explain how lengthy and unpredictable permitting processes can drive up costs for American consumers and leave the U.S. more reliant on foreign resources needed to power the economy. Rep. Westerman discusses his SPEED Act, which passed the House in December and awaits a vote in the Senate. The bill would modernize NEPA to help streamline the permitting process, shorten timelines, and reduce the frequency of frivolous litigation, while maintaining environmental and labor standards.

The Congressmen also talk about the importance of expanding domestic production of energy and critical minerals, particularly as demand for resources continues to grow. A more predictable permitting process would give American companies greater certainty to invest, build, and create jobs at home. Reps. Stauber and Westerman underscore the need to pass meaningful permitting reform before the 119th Congress ends to ensure America can build and produce what it needs at home.

You can listen to the full episode on Spotify and Apple Podcasts.

Read highlights from the conversation below:

Rep. Pete Stauber (MN-08): “Can you tell us about the SPEED Act and why it is important to us? You and I both serve on the Natural Resources Committee…Can you talk about the SPEED Act, its particulars, and how we continue to get across the Senate?”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “It’s hard to build things in America…And when we talk about building things, we're talking about infrastructure, roads, bridges, navigable waterways, railroads, pipelines, all of that kind of infrastructure. It’s just very cumbersome to build it…We want to be able to go through the process in a timely manner, and that has all kinds of positive implications. It gives investors confidence. It keeps us on the front edge of production and technology…If you look at all the things that were invented in the United States, and it happened because people knew they could have an idea and they could make it work, and what the current regulatory structure has done is put a wet blanket on American innovation, on using our own natural resources. It’s made us dependent on other countries for critical minerals. It’s made us dependent on other countries for the resources that we have, that we could be using to make Americans’ lives better, both in having good jobs and building strong communities, and also in making the cost of everyday goods less.”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “It’s also discouraging to see how much better our country could be if we had a streamlined permitting process. And we know that we build things here in America better than anybody else. We protect human rights. We protect the environment, and we can’t keep exporting our environmental guilt to some other country that’s actually doing a worse job with the environment. Because when we export that environmental guilt, we’re also exporting jobs, we’re exporting wealth, and we’re destroying rural communities.”

Rep. Pete Stauber (MN-08): “We need these critical minerals. It’s national security. And if we had the SPEED Act into law, that would reduce the timelines to be able to get a mine up and running without compromising the environment or labor standards.”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “NEPA is a process. We want to go through the process, but we want to make the process happen more quickly…After you’ve gone through the whole NEPA process, got your record of decision, like right now in the law, you’ve got six years where you can file a suit and a judge can issue an injunction and stop the project…We saw this in Arizona. Yep. An activist comes along, files a lawsuit. A sympathetic judge says, ‘Okay, I’m going to issue an injunction.’ So, like the Resolution Copper mine in Superior, Arizona, they spent decades getting it permitted, spent $2 billion…A lawsuit was filed, stopped development of the copper mine, which is a critical mineral that’s needed like no other right now, and just this year, in 2026, they were able to start back on the mine again.”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “This is bipartisan. Some of the time restraints were brought to us by Democrat Members. And everybody recognizes that we need fair permitting. And this is not favoring one technology or one project over the other. So if you’re developing renewable energy or if you’re developing fossil fuels, it’s the same permitting process and you get a fair shake and you don’t get the heavy hand of one administration versus a heavy hand of another administration, we call that permitting ping pong.”

Rep. Pete Stauber (MN-08): “It’s a bipartisan piece of legislation which is really good for all industries. And, you know, we can talk whether it's the oil and gas industry, wind or solar, the mining, forestry, transmission lines, etc. all that [the] SPEED Act will help every single industry across this great nation…We want to make sure that we can get it across the Senate. Like you say, time is running out in this 119th Congress.”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “Americans have created a system where theoretically you have a fair shake, you have a fair chance. You get to try your ideas, you don’t get to side step environmental laws or anything like that. You play with the rules. But we’ve got a system now where you can’t play by the rules. The rules are stacked against Americans that are wanting to innovate, Americans that are wanting to do good, to make us more secure, to make us more economically viable. And it can’t happen under this regulatory process. And we’re seeing businesses close. We’re seeing foreign competitors take advantage of our environmental laws and manipulating our markets. And it just shouldn’t be that way. We should allow Americans to compete on a global market and to be able to do what we’ve always done, and that’s innovate.”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “ [In] 1995, we produced three times more copper than China. Today, they produce 11 times more copper than we do. We have two copper smelters and they have over 60. It’s not because we don’t have copper deposits in the U.S. It’s because we quit mining and refining copper and we know the economic impacts…Just our mining sector alone, with $140 billion of raw material per year, provides a $4 trillion impact to our economy.”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “We have abundant oil and gas. We have the ability to produce more electrical generation from multiple kinds of sources. We could be generating nuclear power. We could be innovating and leading with battery technology so that you could have grid level battery storage and make some of these renewable technologies more efficient. But if we can’t innovate and build, and if we don’t have the resources to do that, that puts us at an extreme disadvantage.”

Rep. Pete Stauber (MN-08): “Like by 2040, we’re supposed to, all experts say, we’re going to use twice as much copper by 2040 than we’re using today. Where are we going to get that? Let’s do it here. The good Lord blessed the United States…with these minerals.”

Rep. Bruce Westerman (AR-04): “If you’re concerned about cost of living, think about when we’re not making this stuff in America anymore, and a foreign country determines what the prices are going to be. That’s right. And they don’t have a public service commission or people that are out there looking at it saying, no, that’s too high. You’re gouging the consumer…They’re going to use their control of resources to bankrupt our country if we keep going this way.”

Dive Brief:

A U.S. District Court judge for the District of Columbia on Tuesday ruled that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency illegally terminated the $7 billion Solar for All program in a lawsuit brought by Harris County, Texas, last October.

The decision comes less than a week after the U.S. District Court of Rhode Island on Friday ruled the EPA’s termination of the Solar for All program was procedurally unlawful in a lawsuit filed on behalf of downstream beneficiaries of Solar for All grants.

The EPA is reviewing both decisions and considering options for appeal, it said in emails to Smart Cities Dive. A third lawsuit contending the grant cancellation was illegal, filed by 22 states and the District of Columbia in U.S. District Court in the Western District of Washington last October, was dismissed in January.

Dive Insight:

The Texas Solar for All Coalition was awarded nearly $250 million in 2024 to expand solar access across the state as part of the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund established by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. Harris County — the state’s largest county and home to Houston — led the coalition and secured more than $54 million.

The EPA eliminated the program in August 2025, citing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, but the lawsuit states “the OBBBA provides no authority for EPA’s Elimination Decision.”

District Court Judge Tanya Chutkan wrote in her Sept. 22 ruling that EPA’s decision to eliminate the Solar for All program without congressional authorization was “arbitrary and capricious, contrary to law, and in excess of statutory authority.”

That decision applies to the EPA’s cancellation of all Solar for All grants, not just Harris County’s, Chutkan ruled. “What the court sets aside is the agency’s policy-level determination that OBBA rendered continued operation of SFA legally impermissible — [which is] applicable to the program as a whole,” she wrote.

The EPA’s termination of Harris County’s Solar for All grant and the resulting legal fight have set the county back in building clean energy initiatives to help low-income households save on energy costs, create jobs and establish solar-powered community hubs for the county to use in the event of power outages and state grid failures, according to a Harris County news release.

“This is a really important victory for energy resilience in Harris County,” Harris County Judge Lina Hidalgo said in a statement Wednesday. “The fight continues but this is a big step to getting our funding back.”

(COLUMBUS, Ohio)—Ohio Governor Mike DeWine today announced that the U.S. Department of Energy (U.S. DOE) has awarded Ohio a $273 million grant to update Ohio’s existing high-voltage electric infrastructure via the Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades (SPARK) initiative.

“Upgrading existing infrastructure makes sense, and this grant opportunity allows us to do that," said Governor DeWine. "Ohio, like much of the country, is facing increasing electricity demand over the next decade. Thank you to the Trump Administration and Secretary Chris Wright for this funding that will help Ohio meet the needs of our businesses and our citizens.”

As part of the total grant award, Governor DeWine announced $137 million is being allocated to the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (PUCO) to work with transmission utilities to implement advanced transmission technologies to increase the capacity of the transmission grid, allowing it to carry more energy, rather than build new infrastructure.

PUCO identified that upgrades made from this grant can add the equivalent of 5,820 megawatts of capacity to the grid, effectively displacing the need to build additional power plants or transmission lines.

“As Ohio and the nation work to restore traditional domestic manufacturing and bring large loads onto the system, we need a strong and robust energy grid," said PUCO Chair Jenifer French. "We are so appreciative of the funding from the U.S. DOE that will allow Ohio to deploy advanced transmission technologies, ensuring that we responsibly and affordably enhance the grid.”

Ohio has laid the groundwork for deploying advanced transmission technologies through the enactment of House Bill 15 in 2025. The PUCO published a report on opportunities from advanced transmission technologies.

text:
In London, on June 10, North Carolina’s coastal insurer of last resort made history. For Don Hornstein, the Thomas F. Taft Distinguished Professor of Law and director of the Center for Climate, Energy, Environment, and Economics, it was the culmination of a 15-year vision. On June 10, the world’s first resilience catastrophe bond, a $600 million innovation that Hornstein helped design, won Initiative of the Year at a black-tie gala attended by more than 300 of the world’s top international insurance specialists.

In many ways, this was no surprise. More than a year earlier, in May 2025, Carolina Law’s student-run Environmental Law Project won Pro Bono Project of the Year for the work of more than a dozen law students who confirmed that this resilience catastrophe bond would indeed be the world’s first such financial product. You can see a photo celebrating the students’ 2025 award here.

The Journey Begins

The road to international recognition began in 2008, when Hornstein was appointed by the North Carolina General Assembly to solve a problem that has become all too familiar: insurers leaving coastal areas because they weren’t allowed to charge enough in rate to withstand losses caused by increasingly volatile weather. Hornstein accepted the appointment with a clear insight: the only way to break the cycle of rate increases and insurer insolvencies was for insurers to promote and reward climate-resilient construction. Study after study had shown that resilient construction more than paid back the investment, often many times over.

In the 2008 legislative study commission, Hornstein, aided by the work of his research assistant Daniel Peterson ’10, pitched an idea that would soon take root: authorizing North Carolina’s newly designed coastal insurer of last resort, the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association, to create its own affirmative mitigation program. In 2009, the General Assembly enacted House Bill 1305 with statutory language that authorized the new entity to do exactly that.

Almost immediately, Hornstein was appointed by Wayne Goodwin, the state’s commissioner of insurance, to the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association’s board of directors. Within a few years, Hornstein and Gina Hardy, the association’s CEO, began laying the groundwork for storm-ready construction at the North Carolina coast, partnering with the Institute for Business and Home Safety, the insurance industry’s research facility dedicated to improving home resiliency. Institute for Business and Home Safety had designed better-than-code roof upgrades known as Fortified roofs. In test after test at Institute for Business and Home Safety’s wind tunnel outside Charlotte, the largest such facility in the Western Hemisphere, Fortified roofs regularly outperformed even brand-new code roofs.

In November 2016, the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association’s board authorized the launch of its first resilient-building program, providing a free “endorsement” to policyholders on the Outer Banks and Barrier Islands: whenever they were entitled to a roof replacement, the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association would install an upgraded Fortified roof at no additional charge. Almost immediately, Hornstein was asked by the Obama White House to fly to Washington, D.C., to explain the initiative, which the White House Office of Management and Budget soon recognized as breaking new ground on insurer-led climate resilience. One week later, the World Bank asked Hornstein to brief its policymakers on the development. He recounted all of it in a TEDx talk at the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics. In the years since, the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association has expanded on that first program, investing $130 million to install more than 20,000 Fortified roofs on the North Carolina coast, the largest such investment in resilience by a single insurance company in the world.

The Moonshot: Creating a New Financial Instrument

Like many insurers, the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association purchases reinsurance (insurance for insurance companies), as well as an analogous financial product known as an insurance-linked security catastrophe bond as a source of ready capital in the event of significant storm-related losses. In 2015, Hornstein read a Brookings Institution report by Dr. Shalini Vajjhala speculating that insurance-linked security catastrophe bonds could be designed to help finance climate resilience investments. But for the next decade, no one in the insurance world had found a way to make an insurance-linked security catastrophe bond a reality. As the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association’s investments in storm-resilient housing grew, Hornstein became convinced they could provide the bedrock for exactly such a financial product.

In summer 2024, Hornstein took the first steps to make it happen. He began with an invited lecture on July 4, 2024, in London at the offices of Marsh McLennan, the world’s largest insurance consultancy, where he first linked the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association’s resiliency investments to the type of insurance-linked security catastrophe bonds Dr. Vajjhala had envisioned. In August, he contacted Cory Anger, a senior manager at Guy Carpenter Securities in New York City, to enlist her help. Anger, in turn, brought in Tom Beckmerhagen, the principal lead underwriter at Hannover Re, one of the largest reinsurers in Germany. Together, Anger and Beckmerhagen flew to Raleigh in September 2024 to meet with Hornstein, Gina Hardy and other North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association executives for lunch at Seasons 52 in Crabtree Valley Mall. There, over lunch, the group sketched out the key financial terms of the world’s first insurance-linked security catastrophe bond for the first time.

Within six months, Hornstein, Hardy and the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association’s financial team flew to New York City, London and Zurich, pitched the Association’s new resilience catastrophe bond, and secured $600 million in investments. By spring 2025, the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association had launched the world’s first resilience catastrophe bond. Artemis, the Bermuda-based news outlet covering the reinsurance and catastrophe bond world, captured the significance of the launch.

Carolina Law’s Newest Center, and Where Things Go From Here

In 2025, Hornstein was asked to take over the Center on Climate, Energy, Environment, and Economics. One of his first requests was to seek University permission to rebrand the center so that, in addition to energy law and environmental law, it would also specialize in the kind of insurance-linked climate resiliency work he and Environmental Law Project students had been pursuing. The University granted that permission in fall 2025, the same time Hornstein secured funding to hold Carolina Law’s first conference on insurance-linked investments in climate resiliency.

That conference took place Oct. 23-24, 2025, drawing more than 150 attendees to the Carolina Club to hear from a who’s-who of experts: Dr. Vajjhala, whose Brookings paper inspired it all; representatives of the world’s largest reinsurers; financing specialists from the World Bank, the Nature Conservancy, and Marsh McLennan; Gina Hardy and North Carolina Insurance Commissioner Mike Causey; and Cory Anger, Tom Beckmerhagen and Hornstein.

Since then, there’s even more to report. Carolina Law has secured funding for a second, even larger conference, to be held at the Carolina Inn on Friday, Oct. 9, where Hornstein, Dean Hessick and Carolina officials will formally announce the Center on Climate, Energy, Environment, and Economics’s transformation into the new Center on Risk, Resilience, Energy, and the Environment. This year’s conference will report further on North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association-led breakthroughs in the insurance-resiliency connection and add a two-hour afternoon session on energy law. The Clean Energy Fund Carolinas will report on its recent $4 million investment from the North Carolina Insurance Underwriting Association to install Institute for Business and Home Safety super-roofs for low-income policyholders who can then qualify for additional energy-efficiency funding. The session will also cover the energy and insurance demands of AI data centers, a hot topic ahead of the fall elections, along with innovations in distributed energy resources in North Carolina and beyond.

text:
Senate Minority Leader Rob Ortt Meets with EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin in Washington, D.C.

Washington, D.C. - Yesterday, New York State Senate Minority Leader Rob Ortt traveled to Washington, D.C. to meet with Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin regarding the discovery of elevated radiation levels in the Town of Niagara and surrounding areas of Western New York.

During the meeting, Senator Ortt spoke with Administrator Zeldin about the latest developments affecting local homeowners and stressed the need for continued federal leadership, accelerated testing and remediation, clear communication with residents and government partners, and stronger coordination between the EPA, the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, and Department of Health.

Senator Ortt also used the meeting to underscore his efforts within the state legislature to push for the passage and signing of his bill, Senate Bill S.10672, which would expand New York State’s Superfund program to include radioactive and radiological waste. Under current state law, New York’s Superfund includes various hazardous and toxic wastes, but explicitly excludes radiation.

“From the beginning, I’ve committed myself and my office to advocating for affected residents, and assisting them in connecting with EPA, DEC, and DOH resources. I’ve been on the ground and met with families whose homes and properties are spiking radioactive levels off the charts - nobody should have to live like this,” said New York State Senate Minority Leader Rob Ortt. “Administrator Zeldin is fully aware of our situation, and agrees that my bill is a common sense solution that would give our state more tools to quickly and effectively test and remediate radioactive properties.”

“The Trump EPA has been working tirelessly to address potential radiological contamination in western New York and protect the health of residents,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin.

“We’ve surged resources into the region and have worked to ensure maximum transparency with impacted residents and the public. Make no mistake, this is a top priority for us and we’re committed to coordinating with the state until the job is done.”

In the coming days, Senator Ortt plans on directly contacting affected residents to thoroughly discuss details of the meeting with Administrator Zeldin.

“I’d like to thank Administrator Zeldin for meeting with me, the outstanding work they are doing regarding this situation, and for making Western New York a priority,” closed Minority Leader Rob Ortt.

text:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul recently announced the Energy Infrastructure Development Plan (EIDP), an updated framework for New York’s energy planning process focused on investments in energy infrastructure that will ensure system reliability and meet project demand in the coming decades. The September 22, 2026, announcement describes the EIDP as “an actionable blueprint designed to cut through red tape and match resources with economic growth.”

The EIDP aims to achieve project development and grid expansion objectives by leveraging neighborhood-scale alternatives, distributed solar, and energy storage, while focusing on the development of new utility-scale clean generation and transmission infrastructure. The EIDP’s focus on investments in statewide energy infrastructure is intended to address ratepayer concerns over affordability and plan for near and long-term large load growth from manufacturing, electrification, and Artificial Intelligence.

Governor Hochul is directing the New York State Planning Board to begin the EIDP process later this year as part of the next State Energy Plan. The EIDP’s focus on infrastructure investment follows the adoption of the 2025 New York State Energy Plan, a comprehensive policy document guiding energy planning through 2040 amid the State’s continued efforts to meet the goals of the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act (CLCPA). Both emphasize cost and reliability as key priorities in New York State’s energy policy.

An interim EIDP will be due in 2027, and the first comprehensive EIDP will be finalized by December 2029. New York will then carry out new EIDPs in the future as part of the ongoing State Energy Planning process.

The EIDP announcement comes during Climate Week and is part of the Clean, Highly Affordable, Reliable Grid Expansion (CHARGE) Agenda, a five-pronged initiative designed to implement New York’s transition to renewable energy sources while protecting affordability for customers. The CHARGE Agenda aims to reduce energy costs for New Yorkers through funding a $1 billion rebate program, implementing guardrails on new hyperscale data centers, expanding large-scale renewables, upgrading the state’s transmission grid infrastructure, and creating new clean energy jobs.

Governor Hochul also announced a nearly $1 billion direct investment in building decarbonization and energy cost savings, renewable energy expansion, methane reduction, and agricultural resiliency as part of the CHARGE Agenda. This investment is the second installment in the Sustainable Future Program, which launched in 2025.

name: Louisiana Environment
title: Death by Data Centers - Dissent Magazine
authors: Advait Arun, Aziz Z. Huq, Michael McCanne, Dorothy Slater
description:
Death by Data Centers I’m an oncology nurse in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley.
Across the United States, these data centers are mostly powered by gas or coal.
Even without these new data centers, Louisiana has seen enough death and destruction.
“I think it’s the data centers too.
I drive all over the state for work, and farmers are all selling their land so the data centers can be built there instead,” he says.
text:
Death by Data Centers

I’m an oncology nurse in Louisiana’s Cancer Alley. My patients and I breathe the same polluted air, and we can’t afford the toxic exposure from the gas-fired plants set to power the state’s proposed AI data centers.

My patient is throwing up when I enter the room. There are beads of sweat on her head; her brow is wrinkled with fear. I place a cool washcloth on her neck. “It’s OK,” I say. “It will pass. I’m here with you. I’ll be right back with an anti-nausea medicine. You don’t even have to swallow it. I can push it through your IV.”

I walk out of the room, always quickly, because there are a dozen other things to do. I try to pull her medicine from the electronic dispenser without anyone interrupting me. I don’t want to let my patient wait. I make it back to the room, draw it up in a syringe, and flush it into her body, slowly now, because pushing it too quickly can cause heart dysrhythmias.

I look up at the television in her room and see a commercial from Meta, spotlighting people in small-town Louisiana who are seemingly thrilled to have one of the world’s largest data centers built in their neighborhood, so thankful for the jobs it will apparently bring. I look back at my patient, who is stuck here in the hospital with cancer, as rage rises inside me.

I am an oncology nurse in “Cancer Alley,” the gorgeous, haunted eighty-five-mile stretch of the Mississippi River between New Orleans and Baton Rouge, Louisiana. This section of the river alone is stuffed with around 200 oil, gas, and petrochemical operations, making up 25 percent of U.S. petrochemical processing. The chemicals involved in the industry are deadly: Almost every census tract on this stretch ranks among the top 5 percent for cancer risk from toxic air pollution, over forty-seven times what the federal government has deemed acceptable and, in some places, seven times the national average. Already at the frontlines of the cancer-causing petrochemical industry, Louisiana now faces a new wave of AI data center development and, with it, new sources of pollution. Across the United States, these data centers are mostly powered by gas or coal. Meta’s proposed $200 billion data center in Richland Parish, Louisiana, is no different. To support the energy requirements, one utility company, Entergy Louisiana, plans to build ten new gas-fired power plants.

Tech companies like Meta want us to believe that the AI boom is inevitable, and we all might as well get on board. But I’m a nurse, and my job is to advocate for my patients. Even without these new data centers, Louisiana has seen enough death and destruction.

The data centers haven’t infiltrated the cancer statistics yet, but state politicians, including those at the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality, already deny that residents of Cancer Alley face a higher cancer risk. The basis of their claim is a mix of inaccurate measurement and willful lies. State air quality monitoring stations intentionally don’t track the release of several of the chemicals—including formaldehyde, ethylene oxide, and chloroprene—that have been found to most contribute to cancer risk. To further this practice, Donald Trump’s administration proposed a new federal rule in August that would exempt data centers from being required to disclose information about the pollution they create. Additionally, due to patient confidentiality laws, cancer rates are not allowed to be published by geographic area if the underlying population is 20,000 people or less, which applies to many of the small towns where industry has moved in along the Mississippi. While our political leaders may deny the truth, everyone in Cancer Alley knows someone with cancer, often many people—sometimes their whole family.

One patient of mine, who was admitted for last-ditch chemotherapy to hopefully extend her life, was joined by her sister, who slept in the same room to keep her company. She has cancer too. Both of their brothers had cancer. One has died. “I don’t know why we all have cancer,” she tells me. “We never smoked and we tried to eat healthy. The only thing I can think of is that we grew up right next to the Norco power plant.” The town is named after the New Orleans Refining Company, home to an enormous petrochemical plant now owned by Shell and an oil refinery owned by Valero. Plenty of my patients live in Norco—and some of my coworkers too—many of whom know or suspect that they’ve been poisoned.

In March 2026 Entergy announced that the new Meta data center will be powered by seven Meta-funded gas plants, in addition to three other plants that have already been approved. Entergy requested these plants be fast-tracked to avoid the usual review process. The Louisiana Public Service Commission, which has so far aligned itself with Meta, is set to vote on the approval of the seven plants in December. Entergy CEO Phillip May reportedly promised Meta that they could “Use all [the gas] you want, we’ll make more.” Governor Jeff Landry spearheaded the project too, though he and others involved have signed non-disclosure agreements with Meta to prevent information about the project from being available to the public. In a press release from March, a Meta VP thanked him for the state’s business-friendly environment. “Today,” the governor said, “Louisiana once again demonstrates our commitment to capital.”

This commitment has a long history, and has come at the cost of Louisianans’ lives. Many of the petrochemical facilities dotting this stretch of the Mississippi River were built on the land of former plantations where indigo, sugarcane, cotton, and tobacco were tended and harvested by enslaved Africans and their children. Today, slavery looks different. More than 50,000 people in the state are incarcerated, with many forced to do agricultural work under the blazing sun for pennies.

The neighborhoods in Cancer Alley with the highest cancer risk are disproportionately Black and low-income, communities that the fossil fuel industry has reaffirmed are disposable. Many residents that were displaced by Hurricane Katrina in 2005 were housed in formaldehyde-laden trailers, exposed to dangerous levels of the cancer-causing chemical; the federal government was aware of this and delayed taking action.

Contrary to repeated promises from state officials who claim that new oil and gas infrastructure will bring abundance, this commitment to capital has not trickled down to benefit the rest of us. Louisiana is the poorest state in the country, with nearly 19 percent of the population living under the federal poverty level. Organizations like Rise St. James, Inclusive Louisiana, Louisiana Bucket Brigade, Concerned Citizens of St. John, and other fierce advocates have worked for years to educate residents and block these developments.

I have a new patient with a suspected diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia. New patients are always tough for me. They’re not used to being in a bed for weeks on end, disturbed every hour with no expectation of privacy. I think back to one of my first patients, a tough old Cajun man who teared up when I described the likely course of treatment. “I’m an outside guy,” he told me in quiet protest. I get it. The fluorescent lights, the startling lack of fresh air, the Styrofoam water cups are all oppressive even to me, and I get to leave every night.

This new patient is friendly, but I enter the room at an inconvenient moment. He’s on the phone planning his sister’s funeral. She died this morning, he says. Cancer. He tells me that his aunt died last week too—also from cancer—so they have a lot of funeral planning to do. He doesn’t say it, but I sense his fear. Here he is with a new cancer diagnosis. I stay quiet to respect the enormity of it all. He breaks the silence: “There’s a DuPont chemical facility near my house.” Oh. I look at him squarely in the eyes to show that I see him before he goes on. “I think it’s the data centers too. I drive all over the state for work, and farmers are all selling their land so the data centers can be built there instead,” he says. “Y’all are going to need a bigger hospital.”

He’s right. This spring, we had twenty-nine beds in our oncology unit, but the hospital has invested in a massive expansion so by the end of September, we will have fifty-three. From the windows of our unit overlooking the Mississippi River, I can see several petrochemical plants with mysterious fumes leaving their smokestacks. As their numbers grow, so do ours.

I ride my bike to and from work along the levee holding back the river. The ride gives me time to prepare for the day, or to let its heartbreaks and traumas settle before I arrive home in the evening. In the winter, my commute is lit by moonlight and the glow from the petrochemical plants, which never sleep. In the summer, it’s beautiful and humid, but I can smell the chemicals. I try to shake off the suffering I’ve witnessed. I breathe in and out, aware that each inhalation brings carcinogens into my own body. It’s suffocating to know that clean air is not available for me, my patients, or any of the people I love. I even feel sorry for the cicadas chirping nearby.

One of my patients was a stubborn man whose cancer had swollen his neck, face, and tongue. He was only able to breathe through a tube. He wanted a drink of water, but, with the swelling, there wasn’t room in his throat for a single drop. I wet a piece of gauze for him, and he squeezed it onto his tongue, then used it to anoint himself—a silent prayer in a cramped hospital room when his family wasn’t looking. He died at the end of my shift. His two children screamed and filled the hallways with their tears. His son, between angry sobs, told me and only me: “He didn’t even get to go outside. I wanted to take him outside.” I went home, past the gas plants, with that memory in my throat.

Dorothy Slater (she/her) is an oncology nurse in New Orleans and a senior fellow with the government watchdog organization Revolving Door Project. Her writing work focuses on political corruption and the destructive impacts of the fossil fuel industry and has appeared in the New Republic, Talking Points Memo, the American Prospect, the Daily Beast, and other outlets. As a nurse, her interests include oncology, palliative, and hospice care. She holds a BS in Nursing and a BA in Political Science. Contact Dorothy at slaterdorothy@proton.me.
