text:
The UK has announced plans to invest £7 billion (US$9.3 billion) into EV battery manufacturing and recycling, but will face a supply gap of 55GWh by 2035.

These are some of the conclusions to be drawn from the latest report from research body New AutoMotive, published this week. ‘The UK’s EV Battery Economy’ looks at announced investments and planned manufacturing capacity in the UK, during a time of strong growth for the country’s EV sector; New AutoMotive figures show that BEVs accounted for 30% of new car registrations in the UK in August, a record figure.

This strong deployment means there is ample appetite for new battery manufacturing work, which has been driven by supportive policy. Chief among these policies is the ZEV Mandate, which came into force in January 2024 and requires vehicle manufacturers to ensure that zero-emission vehicles account for an increasing proportion of sales.

The policy has helped drive more than £41 billion in new automotive investment and the NewAutomotive report notes that while the policy directly governs domestic sales, the UK’s position as an “export-led vehicle producer” means that the incentivisation of more ZEVs on UK roads will, by extension, incentivise further investments in the UK’s manufacturing sector.

Indeed, the report points to the development a 40GWh battery manufacturing factory by Agratas, part of the Tata Group, as a key source for optimism in the UK battery manufacturing space. This facility was facilitated by a £380 million grant from the government’s DRIVE35 programme, which aims to unlock more than £7 billion of private investment over a ten-year period.

Further upstream, the report also points to strength in the UK’s mining sector, which could help secure a domestic supply of some of the minerals and materials necessary to expand domestic EV manufacturing at scale. Projects from Cornish Lithium and Aberdeen Minerals have collectively secured more than £53 million through a combination of public and private funds to develop mining facilities in the regions from which the companies take their name.

NewAutomotive also notes that recycling is a “real strength” of the UK’s EV market, because the UK is and island and is left-hand drive, so UK EVs at the end of their operational lives are unlikely to be exported overseas and will instead be a “captive future feedstock” for component recycling. The report urges the government to continue its policy commitment to the EV sector, most notably through the ZEV Mandate, to take advantage of these factors and build domestic industries that cover the breadth of the supply chain.

UK remains at an ‘early’ stage of battery manufacturing

Despite the causes for optimism, the report notes that the UK battery supply chain is still at an “early” stage of development, and will need significant expansion in order to meet demand for new batteries. The report points to two manufacturing plants—AESC’s operational 15.8GW facility in Sunderland and the Agratas project that is expected to begin commercial operation in late 2027—as the most mature factories in the UK, with a combined output of just above 30GWh.

This is significantly lower than the annual battery demand of 115GWh that NewAutomotive expects by 2035, should the ZEV Mandate remain in place and encourage further uptake of EVs. The automotive sector will account for around 90% of this demand in 2035, and the report estimates that EV production alone will require 35GWh of batteries, more than double the UK’s current operational battery manufacturing output.

This issue is compounded by the dominance of China in manufacturing across the battery supply chain; the report notes that China produces more than 98% of LFP cathodes, over 90% of graphite anodes and up to 90% of battery cells; in addition, east Asian refineries account for 89% of the world’s hard-rock lithium mining. The disparity between the UK and Chinese industries means that the UK is trying to expand its domestic production at a time where a much more established industry is offering similar products to UK buyers.

For this reason, the New Automotive report calls on the UK government to “maintain the demand signal,” as strong policy support for new EV deployment will make it clear that investing in UK EVs, and the domestic manufacturing of these vehicles, has a strong business case for potential investors.

“Gigafactories are built against decade-long demand forecasts,” reads the report. “A stable ZEV Mandate is the single clearest signal the UK can send.”

title: G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Chair's Statement
description:
We recognize that modernizing energy systems, expanding durable energy supply, and improving efficiency can strengthen energy security and support economic growth.
Energy security is strengthened through investments, particularly for developing countries, in energy infrastructure and a diverse range of energy sources and technologies across the entire value chain that address growing energy demand.
Diversify Energy Systems To reliably meet evolving global energy demand, energy systems should incorporate a diversified mix of generation and supporting systems.
A broad range of energy sources and technologies can contribute to meeting today’s rising energy demand.
Strengthen Infrastructure and Resilience Energy systems built on a diversified energy mix require adequate infrastructure and networks that optimally connect energy production to consumers.
text:
We, Energy Ministers of the G20 who assembled in Houston, Texas, in the 250th year of the United States’ independence, affirm that energy security is fundamental to economic growth, national security, and human flourishing. Recognizing the significant effects of the current global energy disruptions in 2026, we reaffirm the importance of secure, resilient, and uninterrupted energy flows, including safe navigation and transit passage through international waterways and the security of critical infrastructure, as essential to global economic stability and energy security. We underscore the importance of timely efforts to support stable, diversified, affordable, and reliable energy supplies and technologies, including through encouraging cooperation to strengthen supply chain resilience. We recognize that modernizing energy systems, expanding durable energy supply, and improving efficiency can strengthen energy security and support economic growth. We note members are pursuing transformation of existing energy systems.

Building an Energy-Secure Future

Each G20 member has a sovereign right to select an energy mix that best serves the needs of its citizens. Promoting access to affordable, reliable, and secure energy is essential for energy abundance. Diversifying supply chains and supporting the transparent flow of energy can contribute to these goals. This is inclusive of a broad range of sources and technologies, including, but not limited to, conventional sources and zero and low emissions technologies, as well as the integration and advancement of transformative energy technologies, as well as modernizing energy systems to improve efficiency and reliability. These technologies can support energy security, sustainability, and reliability. Global energy demand is projected to increase as economies grow, driven by a range of structural factors, including population growth, economic development, industrialization, expanding energy access, electrification, increasing cooling needs, expanding transport demand, and the unprecedented rise of digitalization and information technology. Meeting demand in a manner that addresses affordability, sustainability, accessibility, and security strengthens economic competitiveness and resilience; enhances participation in global markets; and, critically, improves people’s livelihoods, health, and prosperity.

Reaffirming our domestic priorities and respective international commitments, we therefore seek to advance our shared goal of energy security, taking into account the following voluntary principles:

Advance Affordability

Access to affordable energy promotes productivity, increases industrial strength, enhances energy security, generates opportunities for economic growth and development, and improves livelihoods. Targeted policy solutions help address scarcity risks, global market dynamics, and excessive price volatility through adequate investment in energy systems and supply chains to meet evolving demand.

The following efforts further advance energy affordability: implementing demand-side and efficiency measures that complement ongoing supply‑side expansion, especially of the most cost-effective power sources, and do not constrain economic growth; streamlining or eliminating unnecessary regulatory barriers; diversifying sources; optimizing system costs; and fostering predictable investment environments that support stable, long-term planning, including through improving access to affordable financing, particularly for developing countries.

Expand Energy Supply to Meet Structural Demand Growth

Unlocking the potential of domestic energy sources, and the potential of regional connectivity based on mutually agreed terms, will improve universal energy access and help stabilize systems as energy projects scale to meet demand growth, alongside evolving patterns of energy consumption.

Energy security is strengthened through investments, particularly for developing countries, in energy infrastructure and a diverse range of energy sources and technologies across the entire value chain that address growing energy demand. Supply and demand-side measures such as efficient energy use and system flexibility contribute to energy security. Stable and predictable domestic regulatory environments, along with durable contractual frameworks, particularly for long-term agreements, underpin the investments required to expand energy supply.

Diversify Energy Systems

To reliably meet evolving global energy demand, energy systems should incorporate a diversified mix of generation and supporting systems. A broad range of energy sources and technologies can contribute to meeting today’s rising energy demand.

We note emerging energy technologies that can deliver baseload energy. Some countries acknowledge advances in civil nuclear energy technology as contributing to meeting growing global electricity demand and enhancing energy security, while recognizing that, for others, nuclear energy may not be a desired option for their energy mix.

Procurement of energy sources and technologies is strengthened by resilient, reliable, sustainable, and diversified supply chains. Domestic energy mixes will vary based on geography and resource endowments and will reflect domestic policies, including efforts to modernize energy systems, expand reliable, diversified, and affordable supply, and improve efficiency, as appropriate, as well as respective international commitments. Robust analysis based on empirical data and sound science, including the costs associated with inaction, is encouraged when designing policy choices.

Strengthen Infrastructure and Resilience

Energy systems built on a diversified energy mix require adequate infrastructure and networks that optimally connect energy production to consumers. Secure and diversified energy systems call for timely expansion and modernization of transmission, storage, and distribution infrastructure, including cross-border interconnections, where appropriate, such as pipelines and electricity interconnections, supported by sound long-term planning and investment, especially in remote or underserved regions. Robust grid infrastructure strengthens reliability and enables the integration of energy sources and technologies. Approaches to enhance system flexibility and stability include retrofitting, expansion, and modernization of grid backup and balancing capacities.

G20 members encourage exchanges of regulatory best practices and collaboration on improving regulations and permitting to accelerate development timelines, where appropriate, and improve energy outcomes. Recognizing the growing interdependence of energy systems, supply chains, and information networks; and the threats posed to energy infrastructure and supply chains by natural disasters and extreme weather events; G20 members will advance cooperative approaches that protect continuity of supply and strengthen emergency preparedness for resilience to physical, cyber, and hybrid threats, particularly directed at critical infrastructure. Investing in infrastructure development, modernization, diversification, and protection, including in regional interconnections, where appropriate, alongside strengthening connectivity and emergency response mechanisms including fuel reserve systems, safeguards continuity of supply, and mitigates catastrophic outcomes.

Skilled workforces, strong institutional capacity, effective governance, capable and effective regulatory bodies, and engagement among producing and consuming countries and across regions remain critical for system resilience. We also encourage cooperation to strengthen supply chain resilience, address regional vulnerabilities, and foster durable partnerships. We also recognize that wildfires can be significantly impactful to human safety and our natural resources. We encourage voluntary collaboration to share best forest management, fire response training, and emergency management practices, as appropriate.

Enable Innovation

Underlying each of these principles is innovation, which continually strengthens our energy systems and expands future possibilities. G20 members value the promotion of enabling environments that support research, development, deployment, and scaling of a wide range of energy technologies and solutions. G20 members recognize the growing role of transparent, innovative, and market-based approaches that encourage investments that enhance energy security and support diversification. Public-private partnerships can provide an innovative mechanism to finance and develop energy infrastructure, particularly in underserved regions.

G20 members endeavor to catalyze innovation while respecting intellectual property rights and encourage international cooperation and accessible financing as essential to strengthening energy security, and advancing prosperity. We support the deployment of emerging energy solutions and emphasize the role of innovation to support capacity building, particularly for developing countries.

title: Colorado to get $250M in federal funding for electricity grid improvements
authors: Sara Wilson, Jennifer Oldham, Chase Woodruff
description:
The Colorado Energy Office will receive $250 million from the federal government to improve electricity transmission links between Eastern and Western grids, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Thursday.
“By strengthening Colorado’s electric grid and expanding our ability to share power with other regions, we can better protect families and businesses during extreme weather and periods of high demand while continuing to save people money.” Colorado and Oklahoma will get the most federal funds, both at $250 million.
Colorado’s project will “expand interregional transfer capability, improve system reliability, enhance operational flexibility, and strengthen grid resilience across Colorado, Texas, and neighboring regions,” according to a DOE summary.

text:
The Colorado Energy Office will receive $250 million from the federal government to improve electricity transmission links between Eastern and Western grids, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Thursday. It’s part of $1.9 billion total to help fund 31 grid-improvement projects.

“This means lower costs and fewer outages for Coloradans,” Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, said in a statement. “By strengthening Colorado’s electric grid and expanding our ability to share power with other regions, we can better protect families and businesses during extreme weather and periods of high demand while continuing to save people money.”

Colorado and Oklahoma will get the most federal funds, both at $250 million. Some projects, including those in Alabama and Mississippi, are aimed at increasing capacity for large-load data centers, and in total, the 31 projects will add 23 gigawatts of capacity to the country’s transmission system.

Colorado’s project will “expand interregional transfer capability, improve system reliability, enhance operational flexibility, and strengthen grid resilience across Colorado, Texas, and neighboring regions,” according to a DOE summary.

The project will move a transmission connection between Colorado and Texas to the higher capacity May Valley substation in southeastern Colorado. Higher voltage wires will more than triple the amount of electricity that can move between the two regional grids, from 210 megawatts to 700 megawatts. It could one day carry 2,000 megawatts of electricity.

It is part of a larger set of investments to improve the multi-state transmission system, known as the Colorado-to-Texas Western-Eastern Interior Modernization Initiative, or CO2TX.

“Xcel Energy Services Inc’s proposed project will allow optimized use of clean energy resources across a much larger geographical footprint which will save Coloradans money on energy costs,” Will Toor, executive director of the Energy Office, said in a statement.

Because the project involves modernizing existing equipment and lines, it is in line with a March executive order from President Donald Trump that seeks to maximize existing right-of-ways instead of new construction.

“Modernizing the Lamar Tie will strengthen the connection between the Western and Eastern electric grids, helping us better serve customers during extreme weather, meet growing energy needs and make the most of affordable energy resources across the region,” Robert Kenney, president of Xcel Energy–Colorado, said in a statement.

The money was made available through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021. Xcel is contributing an 80% funding match for the project.

name: Louisiana American Energy
title: Guest Column: America's energy strength starts off the Louisiana coast - NOLA.com
description:
In recent years, Gulf lease sales came in fits and starts, with long gaps between sales and years when none happened at all.
Offshore projects require billions of dollars in investment and often take five to seven years or longer to reach first production before supplying American energy for decades.
Consistent leasing supports consistent production, and consistent production helps cushion American families and businesses from the price shocks that accompany geopolitical instability.
Just as important, it provides the long-term certainty companies need to invest in people, training and the skilled workforce that underpins America's energy strength.
It moves through American platforms, American pipelines, American ports and into American markets.
text:
Oil markets have been on edge for months, with prices swinging by double digits some weeks on a single headline from the Middle East, only to settle back down just as fast. Shipping patterns near key chokepoints have shifted too, a sign of how much uncertainty is baked into global supply right now.

Against that backdrop, the federal government held the oil and gas lease sale Big Beautiful Gulf 3 in the Gulf of America on Aug. 12 — the third offshore lease sale mandated under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which restored a predictable Gulf leasing schedule through 2040.

In recent years, Gulf lease sales came in fits and starts, with long gaps between sales and years when none happened at all. The current administration made a deliberate choice to end that uncertainty and restore a predictable leasing schedule that operators can actually plan around.

That decision deserves recognition. Offshore projects require billions of dollars in investment and often take five to seven years or longer to reach first production before supplying American energy for decades. That long investment horizon also means communities need confidence that today's careers will still exist tomorrow.

Affordable energy doesn't begin at the gas pump. It begins years earlier with the policy decisions that determine whether America will have the domestic supply needed to keep markets stable when the next global crisis inevitably arrives. Consistent leasing supports consistent production, and consistent production helps cushion American families and businesses from the price shocks that accompany geopolitical instability. Just as important, it provides the long-term certainty companies need to invest in people, training and the skilled workforce that underpins America's energy strength.

The case for BBG3 grows stronger every time another global chokepoint reminds us how much of the world's energy still depends on someone else's coastline.

The Gulf's advantage is a strategic one. Oil produced off Louisiana's coast doesn't pass through a strait that an adversary can threaten to close, and it doesn't depend on whether a ceasefire holds halfway around the world. It moves through American platforms, American pipelines, American ports and into American markets. The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management estimates the Gulf still contains nearly 30 billion barrels of undiscovered, recoverable oil and more than 50 trillion cubic feet of natural gas, resources that will help meet America's energy needs for decades to come.

The benefits are felt just as strongly here at home.

Every lease awarded today supports years of work for fabrication yards in Houma and Morgan City, marine operators in Port Fourchon, engineering firms in Lafayette and manufacturers throughout Louisiana. Together, these companies form an industrial ecosystem that cannot be switched on and off without consequence.

Predictable leasing gives companies the confidence to hire apprentices, invest in new equipment and develop the next generation of welders, mariners, engineers, geoscientists and technicians. It creates careers that allow families to build stable lives, buy homes, raise children and strengthen their communities.

Predictability also represents long-term opportunity by creating an economy where people of every background, whether they earn a college degree or learn a skilled trade, can build rewarding careers and pursue the American dream. Affordable energy begins with that opportunity. It also keeps federal royalty dollars flowing back to Louisiana's coastal parishes, helping fund wetlands restoration and hurricane protection.

BBG3 is the third sale in a schedule established years ago, designed to deliver production long after today's headlines have faded. Its value extends beyond future barrels of oil and cubic feet of natural gas. It helps preserve an industrial workforce, supply chain and culture of innovation that America cannot afford to lose. The benefits of this kind of policy are measured over decades rather than news cycles.

As America marks its 250th year, it's worth remembering that many of the country's most important strategic decisions shared one characteristic: They invested in capabilities that would serve future generations. BBG3 is one more investment in that tradition.

By reinforcing America's offshore industrial base, supporting Louisiana workers and communities and providing reliable domestic energy for decades to come, this lease sale helps ensure that the next generation inherits not only abundant resources and energy security, but the opportunity to turn those resources into lasting prosperity.

description:

Meanwhile, Türkiye is preparing an emissions trading scheme that could include shipping, while China, Brazil and other countries are developing or expanding maritime emissions monitoring and carbon-pricing frameworks.

text:
The 2026 edition of DNV’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 highlighted this growing uncertainty, with decisions made today on vessel design, retrofits and fuel capability potentially shaping fleet competitiveness for decades.

At the same time, the industry is facing a rapidly changing regulatory landscape, as the IMO continues to develop global measures while the EU and other jurisdictions introduce their own emissions rules and carbon-pricing mechanisms.

“Decisions taken today on vessel design, retrofits, and fuel capability will determine competitiveness for decades, while the outcome of ongoing regulatory negotiations could significantly reshape the economics of shipping’s energy transition,” said Øyvind Sekkesæter, Senior Consultant at DNV and lead author of this year’s report.

For shipowners, this means that investment decisions must increasingly be assessed against a patchwork of current and emerging requirements — not only in terms of compliance, but also fuel availability, infrastructure and long-term commercial viability.

EU and regional rules add pressure to shipping’s decarbonisation drive

While regulatory uncertainty continues at the IMO, the EU is moving ahead with measures that are reshaping the economics of shipping. Since January 2025, FuelEU Maritime has set increasingly stringent greenhouse-gas intensity requirements for ships over 5,000 GT carrying cargo or passengers in the EU and EEA, including 50% of energy used on voyages to and from the region.

The regulation also introduces shore-power requirements and penalties for non-compliance, creating stronger incentives to adopt lower-emission fuels and technologies. Its scope and targets are due to be reviewed by the end of 2027.

The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) has also completed its maritime phase-in. From January 2026, shipping companies must surrender allowances for 100% of emissions within its scope, including CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide.

The system is now under review, with proposed changes including a broader scope, streamlined reporting and financial support for sustainable marine fuels and zero-emission propulsion.

Together, FuelEU Maritime and the EU ETS are already influencing fuel choices and commercial strategies, supporting greater uptake of biofuels and biomethane while encouraging long-term agreements for low-GHG fuels.

Meanwhile, beyond the EU, a growing number of regional and national schemes are adding another layer of regulatory complexity.

The UK ETS began covering larger cargo and passenger vessels from July 2026, while Norway has introduced zero-emission requirements for certain passenger vessels and ferry operations. Djibouti and Gabon have also introduced carbon taxes on part of the emissions from voyages to and from their ports.

Meanwhile, Türkiye is preparing an emissions trading scheme that could include shipping, while China, Brazil and other countries are developing or expanding maritime emissions monitoring and carbon-pricing frameworks.

Although many of these initiatives currently focus on domestic shipping or remain under development, their combined effect is increasing compliance requirements for international operators and adding to the uncertainty surrounding future fleet and fuel investments.

The result is a fragmented regulatory landscape in which shipowners must increasingly account not only for global IMO requirements, but also for a growing patchwork of regional and national rules.

Policies aim to expand low-GHG fuel supply and infrastructure

While emissions regulations remain the primary driver of shipping’s decarbonisation, governments are increasingly using supply-side policies to address another major obstacle: the cost and availability of low-GHG fuels and the infrastructure needed to support their use.

In the EU, the Sustainable Transport Investment Plan (STIP) aims to unlock more than 20 million tonnes of sustainable low-GHG fuels by reducing investment risk, mobilising capital and providing greater long-term market certainty.

The EU’s Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) is also driving investment in alternative-fuel and shore-power infrastructure, requiring relevant TEN-T ports to provide shore power for at least 90% of applicable annual calls by container and passenger ships of 5,000 GT and above by 2030.

China is taking a more long-term, policy-driven approach, using investment programmes and pilot projects to scale up low-GHG fuels. In 2025, its National Development and Reform Commission introduced a scheme offering public funding of up to 20% for low-carbon demonstration projects, including green methanol and fuels produced using captured CO₂.

In the US, support for low-GHG fuel production has been reduced following cuts to tax credits and clean-hydrogen incentives under the Inflation Reduction Act.

However, programmes such as the EPA Clean Ports Program continue to support the deployment of alternative marine fuels and related infrastructure.

Together, these measures are aimed at bringing down production costs, expanding fuel availability and accelerating the infrastructure build-out needed for shipping’s energy transition.

For shipowners, however, the pace and scale of these investments will remain critical in determining which low-GHG fuels can become commercially viable at scale.

text:
Solid majorities of voters on both sides of the political aisle in Colorado’s tightly split 8th Congressional District favor stricter government regulations and tax incentives to combat environmental challenges like air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

That’s according to the latest poll results released Thursday by the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland, which surveyed voters in battleground districts across the country earlier this year — including the one north of Denver pitting Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans against Democratic challenger Manny Rutinel.

“What we’ve consistently found nationally, and now in the battlegrounds, is that large majorities of both Democrats and Republicans want government action to reduce emissions and air pollution using a combination of tax incentives, regulations and international cooperation,” Steven Kull, the director of the university’s Program for Public Consultation, said in a statement.

The 8th District poll, conducted in May and June, included 500 voters. It has found general agreement on a number of hot-button issues among those who lean Republican or Democratic. That has included a wariness of unbridled artificial intelligence development, a desire for a bigger governmental role in healthcare and support for a less draconian approach to immigration enforcement than what the Trump administration has pursued.

A similar bipartisan alignment was discovered when it comes to protecting the environment.

Poll numbers released this week show that 91% of those who lean Democratic and 80% who lean Republican in the district say reducing air pollution should be “a high priority” for the government

Ninety-two percent of Democrats and 70% Republican voters in the district told the pollster that the United States should set a goal of reducing emissions by 2% per year. A similar partisan split (96% among Democratic leaners, 76% among Republican leaners) showed support for the U.S. working with other countries to reduce emissions.

That relative unanimity in a swing district that has elected representatives from both major parties in just the last four years could present problems for Evans, whose party is led by a president who has repeatedly tried to kill wind power projects, has spiked tax credits for electric vehicles and has twice withdrawn the country from the 2015 Paris climate accord.

Rutinel, his Democratic opponent and a former state representative, has attacked Evans mostly on the economic front, where rising energy prices from the Iran war pursued by President Donald Trump have kept inflation at the forefront of the political debate this election cycle.

Rutinel, who resigned from the state legislature this month to focus on his congressional race, once supported a ban on fracking but has since backed off that position. A large portion of the 8th District, which takes in Denver’s north suburbs and Greeley, is in the heart of Colorado’s oil and gas country.

The University of Maryland’s survey also showed that 94% of Democratic-leaning voters and 76% of Republican-leaning voters in the 8th favor tax credits for solar, wind, geothermal and nuclear energy.

Meanwhile, 81% of voters in the district want the government to require that new cars get more miles per gallon of gasoline, with just a 10-percentage-point difference between the large majorities of Democrats and Republicans who feel that way, according to the poll.

Late last year, the Trump administration proposed substantially weakening fuel efficiency standards for new vehicles from the levels the Biden administration established.

text:
The free, open-house-style event is part of the annual National Solar Tour hosted by the American Solar Energy Society October 2-4.

Visitors will have the opportunity to tour a net-zero home, speak directly to an experienced solar installer, and learn how solar power and other renewable energy technologies can work together in a home.

The home features rooftop, pergola, and awning solar, battery backup, electric vehicle charging, three heat pumps, interior daylight features, and air-quality monitoring.

The all-electric home has no propane or natural gas connection and produces enough renewable energy to offset its energy consumption.

Founded in 1954, the American Solar Energy Society is a nonprofit organization that advocates for sustainable living and 100% renewable energy.

Each year, ASES hosts the National Solar Tour to promote renewable energy and increase the adoption of solar energy.

Running from October 2-4 this year in-person and virtual with stops across the country, the National Solar Tour is the largest grassroots solar and sustainable-living event in the nation.

Participants will be able to see solar systems firsthand and talk about installers, financing, regulations, EVs, and more throughout the tour.

For Zook, the tour is an opportunity to build more relationships with those interested in solar and renewable energy in his community.

“We hope visitors leave with a better understanding of what goes into a net-zero home and how all the different systems and technologies work together,” Zook said. “More than anything, we want people to feel comfortable asking questions and exploring what may be possible for their own homes.”

The tour comes as Belmont Solar celebrates its 25th anniversary. Zook founded the company in 2001 after combining solar panels with batteries to create an off-grid power supply.

Since then, Belmont Solar has grown from its off-grid roots to provide grid-tied solar, battery storage, electric vehicle charging, agricultural solar, and other renewable-energy solutions throughout the Mid-Atlantic.

“When we started, there was still so much about solar that we had to learn,” Zook said. “Over the past 25 years, it has been exciting to see our team grow, take on new technologies, and help more people understand what solar can do. Education and personal connections have always been an important part of that work, which is why events like the National Solar Tour are so valuable.”

Visitors can stop by during the open-house hours to explore the home’s energy systems and ask Zook questions about solar power, battery storage, net-zero living, and the considerations involved in bringing renewable energy into their own homes.

text:
NY-17: Second in a series on the environmental stakes of one of the nation’s most fiercely contested congressional races.

Nancy Vann’s resolve has become the subject of a local jingle. Its chorus goes: “If she can do it, so can we.”

Vann, 78, moved to Peekskill, 40 miles north of New York City, after September 11, 2001. Brown & Wood, the law firm at which she worked, occupied five floors of the World Trade Center. She watched both towers fall before her 10:30 a.m. call-in.

Over the next 10 years, her dawn and sunset hours were spent on the Metro-North, a commuter railroad, the Hudson River unspooled alongside.

Vann was no stranger to the Hudson Valley; since the late ‘90s, she had owned a summer cabin in a co-op community in neighbouring Buchanan. Her cabin lay just half a mile from Indian Point Energy Center, a nuclear power plant on the river’s eastern bank. Indian Point, she later learned, had possibly been considered as a target by the 9/11 hijackers.

The nuclear plant, formerly owned by Louisiana-based Entergy, and since acquired by Holtec International, is presently being decommissioned, the years-long process of permanently retiring a facility. How that process is going and what, exactly, it might lead to are points of contention as the Trump administration aggressively pushes a rebirth for America’s nuclear industry.

That debate has become particularly fraught in New York’s 17th Congressional District, where the plant’s future could become an issue in one of the most closely contested House races this November.

Susan Shapiro, an environmental attorney and resident of the district, called Indian Point “the elephant in the room in our region.”

Candidates have opposing views on what should become of the site. Cait Conley, the Democratic challenger, wishes to see the decommissioning progress, while incumbent Republican Mike Lawler, a veteran party official in New York, has advocated for Indian Point’s reopening, and recently took Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright to the site.

“The fact is, there’s no better-positioned site for energy generation in the Hudson Valley than Indian Point,” he told the New York Post in a recent interview.

Nuclear energy sits firmly under Lawler’s “all-of-the-above” energy strategy to improve grid reliability and lower utility costs. Conley, meanwhile, is not decidedly anti-nuclear, but calls the site “broken and decrepit” on her campaign website, which lists “Stopping Mike Lawler’s drive to reopen Indian Point” as a policy priority. A decorated combat veteran and national security official in the Biden administration, she has not publicly taken a position on the plant’s decommissioning.

“I really wanted the Democrats to weigh in on this, but they seemed to be avoiding it,” said Erik Lindberg, a resident of Peekskill.

With Republicans controlling the House by a narrow 218-213 margin, Democrats’ chances for retaking the chamber are considered good—and this district, in the affluent suburbs of New York City, is considered one of their best chances for picking up a Republican-held seat. Whether nuclear power becomes a decisive issue may depend on how voters weigh its potential benefits for energy costs against concerns about public health.

Vann had never paid close attention to Indian Point, or the nuclear issue, until 2014, when she read that Enbridge, a major Calgary-based pipeline company, planned to build a 42-inch gas pipeline beneath her property. It was also within roughly 100 feet of the nuclear plant’s emergency backup generators and switchyard. It was then that she became involved, first in the pipeline fight, then in the battle over Indian Point.

Today, she sits in on six to seven weekly calls about nuclear sites in various stages of transition. There are plants undergoing decommissioning, like Indian Point and San Onofre, in California; others, once slated for closure, that remain in operation, like California’s Diablo Canyon; and “zombie nukes,” like Michigan’s Palisades and Pennsylvania’s Three Mile Island, that are today being brought back online following permanent shutdown. In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul ordered the construction of an “advanced nuclear power plant,” the first in decades.

Indian Point occupies one of the most densely populated nuclear sites in the United States, with roughly 20 million people within a 50-mile radius. The reactors sit near the Ramapo Fault, a minor seismic zone. They used the Hudson River for cooling water and the controlled release of wastewater.

The strong activist base in the community has long made for an activist versus industry dynamic. In turn, they have been blamed for the plant’s closure.

Ultimately, Indian Point’s unsustainable operating costs led to its shutdown in 2021. Entergy also faced years of litigation over the plant’s license renewal, including lawsuits brought by New York State and environmental groups like Riverkeeper.

Over the years, the plant leaked radioactive waste into groundwater, vented an estimated 600,000 gallons of radioactive steam into the atmosphere, spilled some 3,000 gallons of dielectric fluid and 100 gallons of oil into the river and on occasion raised nearby water temperatures by 15 degrees, killing fish and triggering environmental concerns.

A recent study led by Harvard University’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health found higher cancer mortality rates in counties near operating nuclear plants.

Seven years after moving to Peekskill, Vann was diagnosed with duodenal cancer, a rare and aggressive disease; doctors discovered a grapefruit-sized tumor in her small intestine. She has also had seven cats die, each from cancer.

“It doesn’t prove anything,” Vann said. “But it leaves a bad feeling.”

Then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo pushed to shutdown Indian Point despite the plant providing high-paying, unionized jobs, 400 of which were lost when it closed. Unions today form a key part of Lawler’s political base, in a district where a third of residents live in a union household.

A fund intended to cushion communities from the loss of Indian Point’s tax revenue—$32 million for local municipalities and school districts—is financed by ratepayers. Lawler has seized on this, and made Indian Point’s closure a campaign issue, accusing Conley of bowing down to climate activists and having no energy plan.

“Reopening the Indian Point Energy Center would restore reliable, affordable, carbon-free energy while reducing our reliance on fossil fuels and lowering emissions,” he wrote in a recent Facebook post, citing a recent report from the New York Public Service Commission.

Indeed, following the closure of Indian Point, New York increased its consumption of readily available gas to make up the shortfall, and electricity-sector emissions rose 22 percent from 2019 to 2022.

The Future of Nuclear Power

The Trump administration has pledged to “reestablish the United States as the global leader in nuclear energy,” with the goal of expanding U.S. nuclear generating capacity from roughly 100 gigawatts in 2024 to 400 GW by 2050.

President Donald Trump’s executive order, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission,” calls for extending the licenses of the existing nuclear fleet and encouraging the “reactivation of prematurely shuttered or partially completed nuclear facilities,” arguing that a stronger domestic nuclear industry is necessary for U.S. competitiveness, particularly with China.

In response to Trump’s executive orders, the Department of Energy revised its process to expedite the review, approval and construction of advanced reactors. The new standard allows applicants and the DOE to “negotiate” requirements to achieve safe and secure design, construction and operation as efficiently as possible, “using the minimum requirements necessary” to meet that goal.

The administration’s approach has drawn criticism from former regulators. Gregory Jaczko, who chaired the NRC under President Obama, said the executive order looked “like someone asked an AI chatbot, ‘How do we make the nuclear industry worse in this country?'”

Despite a 2026 report by the Government Accountability Office that recommends the NRC address its shortcomings in considering the risk increase from climate change as part of its license renewal process, the NRC voted 3-2 against adopting recommendations to more comprehensively evaluate these risks.

“The NRC is driving the licensing process through the rearview mirror,” said Paul Gunter, a nuclear reactor specialist and director of Beyond Nuclear, a nonprofit which advocates ending the use of nuclear power.

For opponents of Indian Point’s closure, the administration’s pro-nuclear power policies have renewed speculation about the future of the site. Wright has called the plant’s closure “a foolish political decision,” raising questions over whether Indian Point could be considered one of the “prematurely shuttered” facilities eligible for revival. Doing so, however, would require approval from five parties—the Village of Buchanan, the Hendrick Hudson School District, New York State, Westchester County, and the Town of Cortlandt—the latter three of which have stated their opposition.

Even as concerns over costs, safety and decommissioning remain, investment in nuclear energy is accelerating. Meta, Microsoft and Google are among the companies looking to nuclear power to meet the energy demands of artificial intelligence, despite the industry’s long construction timelines and high costs.

“Nuclear power of any size, small or large, is going to face the same problems of the inability to reliably control the cost and control the time in which they can project to finish. And these are two key factors that are antithetical to addressing climate change,” said Gunter.

Holtec’s Decommissioning of Indian Point

Vann’s voice has a slight waver. Speaking on the future of Indian Point, it doesn’t falter.

“There are two signed contracts,” she said, referring to agreements with Entergy and Holtec that require unanimous consent before the site could be revived for nuclear generation. “For Mike Lawler to stand there, at Indian Point, and call for its reopening, he is saying they will ignore the law. He cannot do that. And we will take them to court if they try.”

At most hurdles, Vann’s recourse is the law. She is not shy about taking matters to court. This resolve is steeped in her steadfast belief that law, the Constitution, will, and has, delivered American progress.

Vann is now involved in the oversight of the plant’s decommissioning by Holtec, a company specializing in spent-fuel storage, small modular reactors and, more recently, nuclear plant decommissioning. Holtec acquired the plant from Entergy in 2021 despite Attorney General Letitia James filing to intervene, stating Holtec did not “possess the financial qualifications necessary to complete such a risk-intensive project.”

Decommissioning involves removing nuclear fuel, cleaning up radioactive contamination, dismantling structures and releasing the land for other public or industrial uses. Holtec has overseen this work, and the $2.3 billion-plus trust fund financed by utility customers that pays for it, with some opacity.

Residents and activists say they feel left out of decision-making, unsure how their money is being spent. A decommissioning oversight board exists to monitor the process, but critics question whether it has provided sufficient scrutiny. Former Gov. Cuomo directed the New York State Department of Public Service to establish the board to protect the financial, environmental and physical interests of local communities affected by the plant’s closure.

“It’s like a shotgun marriage. Some things, they are very forthcoming on, others, like the trust fund, they are not,” said New York State Sen. Peter Harckham, a Democrat, who represents the area and serves as chairman of the state Senate Committee on Environmental Conservation.

“We see the balances have gone down significantly. What was that spent on? Is that a typical expenditure for this point in the process? It’s hard to get clarity,” he added.

Since 2021, the fund has declined by approximately 32 percent. Holtec’s estimated completion date stretches into 2062.

What Comes Next?

The federal government’s increasingly pro-nuclear stance has already affected Indian Point’s decommissioning, state officials say.

“After the federal election two years ago, it’s a whole new NRC crew, and they are much less committal than the last group,” said Harckham.

“I don’t know whether that’s going to be a process of just establishing mutual trust or if it reflects the political focus of the new administration: pro-nuclear, and communities be damned,” he added.

However, despite Hochul’s broader support for expanding nuclear energy, she has remained opposed to reopening Indian Point, and any future nuclear use of the site would require state approval.

Shapiro notes communities’ reliance on the NRC’s proactive environmental protection standards.

“With the NRC basically abdicating all responsibilities, the state has to provide the oversight,” she said. “In every state, I think nuclear power will become a state’s rights issue.”

Holtec has never completed a nuclear power plant decommissioning project. That worries critics who question whether decommissioning has become a pathway to acquiring reactors as assets rather than dismantling them. Holtec recently filed to go public, in a deal that could raise up to $900 million, and its S-1 filing expresses interest in eventually redeveloping Indian Point as a data center, warehouse or for residential use.

Holtec told Inside Climate News that it is not looking to restart the plant, nor is it in discussions with any developers. “We are evaluating all options … with the focus remaining on the safe, efficient decommissioning of the facility,” a spokesperson wrote.

While most involved in overseeing Indian Point’s decommissioning are unconvinced it could be slated for a restart, the community’s greatest fear is what happens if Holtec burns through the fund before the cleanup is complete.

“That leaves us with a Superfund site that technically is the government’s responsibility, so it becomes our responsibility,” said Lindberg, the Peekskill resident.

Oversight mechanisms are also limited. The local oversight board has neither subpoena power nor any legally binding authority. Holtec is not even required to attend its meetings. Technically, under decommissioning law, the trust fund belongs to Holtec, and while the company must report fund balances, it is not required to disclose transactions.

Those concerns intensified when Holtec announced plans to discharge approximately 45,000 gallons of treated radioactive wastewater into the Hudson River. New York’s Save the Hudson Act, passed in 2023, prohibited the discharge. However, a federal judge later overturned the law, giving Holtec permission to proceed. The decision has since been appealed, but the Trump administration’s weakening of federal Clean Water Act protections has raised additional questions about the appeal’s outcome.

Transparency has also become a point of contention. “After we passed the Save the Hudson Bill, communication with Holtec kind of shut off,” said Harckham.

Vann put it plainly: “They have not been transparent at all,” she said.

On the House race, Vann, an elected member of the Peekskill Democratic Committee, expressed excitement about Cait Conley speaking out on the issue. She was largely impressed with all of the Democratic primary candidates.

“We’re all getting behind Cait because even if she didn’t come out against Indian Point reopening, even if it was still up in the air, Mike Lawler has said he wants to reopen it. It’s a no-brainer.”

Vann has long been a leader in the district’s fight for environmental justice. Her resolve has become the subject of the local jingle—“if she can do it, so can we!”—performed live in bars at fundraisers or during protests over environmental issues.

Robert May, author of the song, describes her as a kind of a “mother hen.”

He remembers her home, the meeting place for organizers of the anti-pipeline campaign, as “command central.” Activists participating in direct action would commute from the city and crash in sleeping bags in her living room.

The movement, she emphasizes, is not about her, or any other individual. Still, that movement has become a voting bloc, challenging those who see a return to nuclear power as the answer to the bipartisan challenge of energy affordability.

Honda Motor Co. plans to build a new hybrid vehicle assembly plant in Ohio, according to reports in Japan but not confirmed by the automaker. A U.S.-based representative for Honda reiterated that "No decisions have been made at ⁠this stage regarding a new plant in the U.S."

The reported Ohio project would have a budget of $1.9 to $2.53 billion, and target a start-up date in 2030, the original report noted.

Recently Honda made it known that a reaffirmation of the U.S. Mexico Canada Agreement on free trade would be a significant factor in determining its capital investment plans.

Hybrid vehicles are taking a prominent role in Honda’s future plans, as it shifts away from battery-electric vehicles. The automaker is actively developing a new generation of hybrid-electric vehicle (HEV) powertrain and vehicle platform, which will be available in new models from 2027 forward.

Earlier this year Honda issued a new “roadmap” for its automotive portfolio, committing to reallocating development and manufacturing resources toward hybrid vehicles due to strong near-term demand. It said it plans to launch 15 hybrid models globally by FY2030, with North America as the primary market.

Currently Honda offers hybrid versions of its Accord, Civic, CR-V, and Prelude models. And a new hybrid system is expected to be introduced in 2027.

In that same statement, Honda explained it will reallocate all excess capacity at its two Ohio assembly to production of gasoline and hybrid vehicles, while make all of its North American assembly plants capable of producing hybrid models.

Honda Motor has seven vehicle assembly plants in North America, two in Ohio, and others in Alabama, Indiana, two in Ontario, and one in Mexico. It also has numerous plants manufacturing engines and engine components, powertrains, and transmissions.

text:
Ottawa is pressing Canada's pension funds to put more capital into domestic industry, including advanced manufacturing. The country's largest planned electric vehicle (EV) battery plant has now pushed its start date back two years.

PowerCo Canada Inc., Volkswagen AG's battery subsidiary, said Sept. 24 that its St. Thomas, Ont., plant will begin operating in 2029 instead of 2027. The company cited evolving market demand, technological advancements and Volkswagen Group's long-term strategy.

"What we really need to understand is this: Is Volkswagen legitimately deferring actual production, or are they deferring a decision on the ultimate utility and necessity of that plant?" said Greig Mordue, associate professor at McMaster University's Booth School of Engineering Practice and Technology in Hamilton.

Billions tied to output

Ottawa agreed in 2023 to provide up to $13.2 billion in production subsidies to Volkswagen over a decade. The Parliamentary Budget Officer later estimated the total federal commitment at about $16.3 billion.

Mordue said the delay could save taxpayers billions because many incentives were tied to production targets and were set to scale back in 2030 before disappearing by 2032. With output starting later and below planned levels, he said, those incentives, "that are measured in the billions of dollars, will not occur."

A pattern of paused projects

Honda postponed its $15 billion Ontario EV and battery project by about two years in May 2025, citing a slowdown in the EV market. Ottawa had planned about $2.5 billion in tax credits for the project, with Ontario committing up to $2.5 billion.

In Quebec, the province ended support for Northvolt's planned battery plant in September 2025 after losing $270 million on its investment in the Swedish parent.

OMERS booked a loss on its $325 million investment, the Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec wrote its $150 million stake down to zero, and IMCO marked down its $400 million investment.

Stellantis's idled Brampton Assembly Plant faces possible closure and sale, which Unifor said this month threatens the wages, pensions and benefits of its members.

Capacity ahead of demand

Mordue said the St. Thomas delay should not surprise anyone following Volkswagen or the North American EV market, adding that a lot can happen in three years and the plant's future is far from resolved.

Earlier this month, Volkswagen said it was looking to cut up to 100,000 jobs worldwide in response to competitive pressures, including weaker sales in China, where Chinese automakers have taken market share.

PowerCo has said the plant could produce up to one million batteries a year. Conrad Layson, a senior analyst at AutoForecast Solutions LLC, said demand and that scale are "well out of line with the vehicles that Volkswagen is looking to produce in North America."

In April, Volkswagen stopped producing its electric ID.4 in Tennessee, one of the main vehicles St. Thomas was meant to support.

Layson said conditions such as the elimination of US EV incentives mean full capacity is likely years away.

Higher gas prices from the war in Iran have renewed buyer interest, and EV sales now account for 5% to 6% of all car sales, below the 8% recorded before 2024.

The cost case for Canadian cells

Layson called the delay puzzling since Canadian cells would cost less than Chinese imports despite US tariffs, though still "hideously expensive."

"However, the cost of importing a Chinese cell versus a Canadian cell is different, and the Canadian cell is lower," he said.

He added the delay spares Volkswagen billions of dollars on a facility that will not approach capacity for years.

Shovels still in the ground

Construction continues under general contractor EllisDon, with the on-site workforce expected to peak at 1,300. Since groundbreaking in 2025, work has moved into core infrastructure and structural phases.

"This is about getting the pacing right – not stepping back – to protect our long-term investment, support regional jobs and position Canada, Ontario and St. Thomas to benefit in a dynamic and evolving market," he said.

text:
Bart Bittner has been adapting to diesel prices all year. The central Illinois farmer relied on fuel he had stored on his farm to run his equipment for as long as he could this spring while diesel prices skyrocketed. When prices fell slightly this summer, he refilled his reserve.

But now he and farmers across the U.S. heading into harvest season are forced to contend with record-high fuel prices during an already economically tumultuous year.

“Of course it’s the worst timing ever, cause this is when we use the most diesel fuel with all the equipment in the field along with the trucks that we have on the road to haul the grain to market,” Bittner said.

A gallon of diesel topped $6 for the first time in mid-September, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. And the price has only gone up since. Across most of the central U.S., diesel prices are averaging $6.68 per gallon. In Texas and other states along the Gulf Coast, the average is $6.17.

Diesel prices had already been on the rise the past few years due to the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine. But prices jumped after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February, blocking the Strait of Hormuz. A quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade goes through the strait, according to the International Energy Agency.

Steep fuel prices are hitting farmers in a year where they’re already contending with other high input costs, said Michael Langemeier, a professor of agricultural economics at Purdue University. Prices for farm equipment and fertilizer have also shot up this year amid the Trump administration’s tariffs and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The only silver lining, many farmers say, is that they’re expecting higher corn and soybean prices this season.

“This would be a huge crisis if we hadn’t seen the increase in crop prices we’ve seen recently,” Langemeier said. “That’s helping. It’s not curing the high input cost problem.”

Some farmers, like Iowa Corn Growers Association President Steve Kuiper, are lamenting that the cost of diesel means these higher prices won’t turn the tide against rising input costs.

“This would have gotten us into a point where we could have been decently making a few bucks,” he said. “And it’s hurting that aspect of it right now.”

Farmers like Bittner in central Illinois are also dealing with the outcome of late summer storms. Bittner said strong wind and heavy rain in August downed about 1,000 acres of corn on his farm.

“That downed corn is gonna require us to actually probably spend more time in the field, which unfortunately translates to probably more fuel to try to get this crop in and do the best we can to harvest as many ears as we possibly can and not lose any more than we have to,” he said.

Transportation costs rise

Tory Meyr is a fourth generation farmer growing corn and soybeans in southeast Missouri. The diesel he purchased to run his farm equipment this year was 60% more expensive than last year, he said, and that doesn’t include the diesel he’ll still need to buy to transport the harvested grain.

“That’s tremendously higher,” he said. “I have three semis that we run, and each one costs about $1,500 to fill up.”

Low levels on the Mississippi River, an important export corridor for corn and soybeans, are also pushing up transportation costs.

“More and more people are vying for that freight, which drives the cost up,” Meyr said, “and then they’re also raising the cost of the freight just because of diesel fuel, which is what the tugboats run on.”

These increased costs are heavily influencing where, how and when farmers transport their harvest, said Kuiper with the Iowa Corn Growers Association. He said many producers are reconsidering grain storage plans this year.

“You might bring it to a more local elevator then bring it further away because added fuel costs,” he said. “You don’t gain that much of a price difference if you’re having to drive further.”

For Meyr, that means holding off on transporting his harvested crop — at least until the Mississippi River is higher. He’s planning to keep his grain in storage on his farm and haul it later in the winter.

In the meantime, Meyr said he is trying to cut down on diesel use any way that he can.

“It’s 97 degrees today, so when they’re waiting to get filled by the grain cart, normally we’d just let them run, so the guys can sit in the air conditioning,” he said. “But we’re turning them off, so they’re not running all day long while they’re waiting to be filled each time.”

Planning for next season

There’s not much farmers can do at this point in the season to avoid high diesel prices, but many are considering ways they can use less fuel after harvest.

Ben Brown, a senior research associate and extension agricultural economist at the University of Missouri, thinks a lot of farmers will take the approach of doing less field work in the fall and spring to bring down diesel use.

“I also think we’ll see fewer chemical applications,” he said. “So instead of maybe a two-pass crop protection in the growing season, maybe just a single-pass and doing a higher rate.”

But that might not be a good option for farmers who have never tried using less chemical applications or reducing tillage, said Ryan Mackenthun. He’s president of the Minnesota Soybean Growers Association and grows soybeans and corn on his farm in central Minnesota.

“It’s really hard to do new things unless you’ve experimented with them before and know their end result,” he said.

Bittner in Illinois said he is planning to reduce the amount of tillage he does this fall. He’s also rethinking how much storage he has on his property for fuel.

“Today we were just making an adjustment and trying to figure out how to maybe get some more storage on the farm so that we have a little more leverage with where we buy it and how we buy it,” he said. “So when we get those opportunities, maybe we can book a little more.”

Langemeier said farmers who have the storage might consider buying some of their fuel now, in case prices continue to rise. Ultimately, he said he doesn’t think diesel prices will come down until the Strait of Hormuz is fully reopened.

“If we can move more through [the strait], the price wouldn’t continue to increase,” he said. “But really if we want to get back to where we were early this year, the conflict in the Middle East at least needs to be resolved.”

text:
See more from Canary Media’s ​“Chart of the Week” column.

Have you ever gazed up at power lines and wondered how clean the electrons passing along them are? The answer is very different depending on where you are.

Just look at the spectrum of blues in the map above. It charts the carbon intensity of power generated in each state in 2024, according to federal data compiled by U.S. Energy Data, a new project from the think tank Institute for Progress. Carbon intensity is the amount of planet-warming carbon pollution emitted per megawatt-hour of electricity generated.

The states with the highest carbon intensity burn a lot of fossil fuels, especially the really dirty kinds like coal and petroleum. In the three states with the dirtiest electricity generation — West Virginia, Kentucky, and Wyoming — most power is created by burning coal, which makes sense considering they are among the top coal-producing states.

States with the lowest carbon intensity, of course, are home to a larger share of clean energy, ranging from wind and solar farms to hydroelectric facilities to nuclear plants. Vermont has the cleanest in-state generation, with essentially 100% of the power it creates coming from renewables — largely hydropower — since 2015.

It’s important to note that the above map represents the power generated in a state — not necessarily the power consumed there. Wyoming, for example, generates about 12 times more power than it consumes. Electricity flows all over the place via sweeping interregional transmission lines — so even a state with a high share of clean power generation could have a dirtier grid than meets the eye.

The good news is that America’s grid as a whole has been getting cleaner over the last two decades. Greenhouse gas emissions from the U.S. power sector fell about 40% between 2005 and 2024 as old coal plants shuttered and were replaced with cheaper natural gas–fired facilities and renewable energy. Generation in all states except Idaho and Vermont got less carbon-intensive over that period of time.

Lots of states want to continue the progress, and many are going so far as to aim for completely clean grids by midcentury. It won’t be easy, as data centers’ energy demand drives a gas power boom and the Trump administration attacks renewables while propping up the coal industry. With the White House stripping the federal climate policies put in place by previous administrations, the onus is increasingly shifting onto states to keep up the pace of the clean energy transition.

authors: Associated Press, Marc Levy and Matthew Daly, Associated Press, Matthew Daly Associated Press, Associated Press), www.facebook.com
description:
ALLENTOWN, Pa. — The Energy Department said Thursday that it will spend almost $2 billion to try to squeeze more electricity out of the nation's aging and stressed power grid, as President Donald Trump's administration steps up efforts to avoid blackouts amid skyrocketing energy demand spurred by artificial intelligence.
The announcement comes amid warnings that AI's voracious demand for power is threatening to overwhelm U.S. power supplies, as massive new data centers come online faster than new power plants can be built.
Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both major political parties criticize them and many communities try to block them.
Trump has vowed to "unleash" the nation's energy sector in his second term, aiming to drive up record-setting domestic oil and gas production, strip away pollution restrictions on power plants and keep expensive coal-fired power plants operating past their retirement dates.
His administration meanwhile has pushed to help tech giants build and connect data centers to power plants and high-voltage power lines and convert Cold War-era uranium enrichment plants into data center and power plant complexes.
text:
ALLENTOWN, Pa. — The Energy Department said Thursday that it will spend almost $2 billion to try to squeeze more electricity out of the nation's aging and stressed power grid, as President Donald Trump's administration steps up efforts to avoid blackouts amid skyrocketing energy demand spurred by artificial intelligence.

The money will go toward 31 projects across 26 states that are expected to produce more than 23 gigawatts of additional electricity capacity — enough to power 16 million homes. The projects will use new technologies such as sensors to measure real-time weather conditions to ensure safe transmission or direct power away from congested paths, the department said.

The upgrades could improve power reliability and lower electricity costs for about 100 million Americans, officials said.

"This is a quick way to lower electricity prices and increase reliability: using fibers that are already in the transmission lines to analyze what's the temperature out, what's the wind out, how can we use this transmission line to distribute more power, but safely and only in the right conditions," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in a news conference promoting the grants Thursday at a PPL Corp. facility in Allentown.

The eastern Pennsylvania electric utility stated two data centers in its territory came online this year, and six more are under construction, with enough other data centers in the advanced planning stages that its peak electric demand could quintuple by 2032.

PPL said it is receiving $71.5 million to modernize an existing high-voltage transmission line across roughly 30 miles in northern Pennsylvania.

The announcement comes amid warnings that AI's voracious demand for power is threatening to overwhelm U.S. power supplies, as massive new data centers come online faster than new power plants can be built. It also comes as electricity bills rise faster than inflation in many parts of the U.S., blamed in some areas on demand from data centers.

The snowballing opposition to data centers in communities across the country has thrown a wrench into the plans of the world's richest companies and transformed the midterm election landscape.

Trump continues to stick up for data centers, even as politicians from both major political parties criticize them and many communities try to block them.

In the meantime, Congress and some states are trying to push utilities to expand their use of new technologies to make grids more efficient and to lessen the need to build new power plants.

Julia Selker, the executive director of the WATT Coalition, a trade association for grid-enhancing technologies, said both the projects and the scale of the investment are significant. Utilities in the U.S. are lagging behind places like Europe in adopting the technologies, despite federal investment in the past to develop and test them, Selker said.

Still, Drew Maloney, CEO of the Edison Electric Institute, a trade association of for-profit utilities, said America's electric utilities are making a "significant investment" every year in new technologies to strengthen the grid and reduce outages.

Wright said that work on the projects should begin right away and that he hoped some efficiencies are in place before this winter to tamp down price spikes when extreme weather sends demand skyrocketing.

Wright said he didn't know whether the projects would have gotten done without federal funding. Many, he said, had been under consideration before the grants were offered, but the grant recipients hadn't "quite pulled the trigger" on them.

Projects being announced Thursday will involve component enhancements on more than 1,500 miles of transmission lines and technological enhancements across nearly 21,000 miles, the department said.

Projects were prioritized based on those that can be put into operation quickly, officials said. Money for the grants comes from the bipartisan infrastructure law enacted by Congress under then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat. The government's $1.9 billion in funding will be matched by $3.35 billion from the recipients, the department said.

Related:

Recipients include utilities, cooperatives and four state agencies. The state agencies — in Colorado, Indiana, Ohio and Oklahoma — were the biggest recipients, collectively drawing $810 million, with the Colorado and Oklahoma projects promising improvements to regional grids.

Trump has vowed to "unleash" the nation's energy sector in his second term, aiming to drive up record-setting domestic oil and gas production, strip away pollution restrictions on power plants and keep expensive coal-fired power plants operating past their retirement dates.

The administration also has pledged nearly $4 billion to buy back offshore wind leases as Trump seeks to discourage the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.

His administration meanwhile has pushed to help tech giants build and connect data centers to power plants and high-voltage power lines and convert Cold War-era uranium enrichment plants into data center and power plant complexes.

text:
“Fusion is the future, and this bipartisan bill is a major step in capitalizing on the promise of its emission-free power,” said Ranking Member Lofgren. “I’m proud to be introducing this bill today alongside Representatives Obernolte, Beyer, Trahan, and Gallagher—and I thank them for their partnership. We are faced with a choice: lead the global race to commercialize fusion power or get left behind. We need to match the momentum we are experiencing with breakthroughs at the National Ignition Facility, from the emerging fusion energy industry, and at universities and other national laboratories across the country to fortify the foundation of fusion energy in America, in both the private and public sectors. With $10 billion in direct investments for high-priority activities, the establishment of an Office of Fusion at DOE, a workforce development program, and much more—this bill will unleash a new era of fusion energy development in the United States.”

“Fusion energy has the potential to be a reliable domestic source of power and strengthen America’s energy independence,” said Rep. Jay Obernolte. “The American Leadership in Fusion Act supports the research infrastructure and commercialization pathways needed to move fusion technologies toward deployment and maintain U.S. leadership in this critical field.”

“Fusion energy can help deliver abundant, reliable, clean energy for decades to come, but if we want to realize its promise, we need to make greater investments in its commercialization,” said Congressman Beyer. “That’s why I’m proud to support the bipartisan American Leadership in Fusion Act, which would provide $10 billion in direct investment to accelerate fusion commercialization and establish an Office of Fusion. We must give promising fusion technologies the resources they need to reach the grid and ensure American leadership in this global race.”

“At a time when families across the country are struggling with rising energy costs, fusion energy offers the promise of delivering clean, reliable, and affordable power. However, turning that promise into reality requires sustained investment and commitment,” said Congresswoman Trahan. “This legislation will help accelerate the commercialization of fusion energy and strengthen America’s position as a global leader in this critical technology. By investing in the scientists, researchers, and companies developing the next generation of energy technology here in the United States, we can advance our clean energy goals, create good-paying jobs, and strengthen our energy independence. America has always been at its best when we lead the world in innovation, and fusion is our opportunity to lead once again.”

“Fusion energy represents a tremendous opportunity to strengthen American energy dominance, drive innovation, and create new opportunities for workers and businesses for the North State and across the nation," said Rep. James Gallagher (CA-01). “This bipartisan bill makes critical investments to accelerate the commercialization of fusion, grow our research capabilities, and support the next generation of American talent. We must build on the breakthroughs happening across our national laboratories, universities, and private sector to ensure America remains at the forefront of fusion energy.”

"The FIA, as the unified voice of the fusion industry, applauds and commends Representatives Lofgren, Obernolte, Gallagher, Trahan, and Beyer for introducing bipartisan legislation to advance the commercialization of fusion energy,” said Andrew Holland, Chief Executive Officer, Fusion Industry Association. “The private fusion industry has attracted a record $4.5 billion in investment over the past year, but to deploy in the U.S. within the next decade, it needs a strong partner in the federal government. The American Leadership in Fusion Act provides the DOE with the necessary guidance to support commercialization, along with the government resources needed to develop the infrastructure and grow the public-private partnerships accelerating fusion's deployment."

“The global race to commercialize fusion will be won by the nation that can translate scientific leadership into industrial strength,” said Ylli Bajraktari, CEO, SCSP Action Program. “The American Leadership in Fusion Actrecognizes fusion as a strategic national priority with the potential to help secure America’s energy future, strengthen its economic and national security, and ensure that the United States—not China—sets the pace for this critical technology. By investing at scale in test infrastructure, milestone-based public-private partnerships, domestic supply chains, and the fusion workforce, this bipartisan legislation translates a comprehensive national strategy into action.”
